title: A Place at the Table
content:

A PLACE AT

THE TABLE

Stories of everyday grace

Prepared for Templar Hughes-Bryant

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

1

These stories are original fiction. Their people and places

are imagined, though the feelings and small acts at their

center may be familiar. Some endings are joyful; some leave

room for grief and hope to live beside each other.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

3

1. The Extra Chair

Every Thursday, Mrs. Bell set a fourth chair at her table.

She lived alone, and her supper guests, two neighbors

from the next building, had never asked why. Sometimes

no one sat there. Mrs. Bell served the empty place a plate

anyway, then scraped it back into the pot at the end of the

meal.

When the new tenant upstairs lost her job, she began

avoiding the hall. Mrs. Bell met her at the mailboxes and

said, "I made too much rice. You would be helping me."

The young woman came downstairs, wary of pity. At the

table she found three people discussing a television quiz

show and one empty chair. Nobody asked for an

explanation of her day.

After supper she offered to wash dishes. Mrs. Bell handed

her a towel. On the way out, the young woman asked

about the chair.

"My mother kept it for anyone who arrived hungry," Mrs.

Bell said. "I used to think it was a waste of space. Then I

needed it once."

The next Thursday, the young woman brought oranges.

She did not have a job yet. She had a place to take off her

coat.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

4

2. The Blue Umbrella

A blue umbrella traveled through Bellwether Station for

six months. At first it belonged to a college student who

left it on the train. A conductor used it to walk an elderly

passenger to a taxi. The passenger gave it to a delivery

rider caught in a storm. The rider propped it outside a

bakery, and a baker handed it to a child whose schoolbag

was soaked.

The child wrote Please pass along on a strip of tape and

wrapped it around the handle. By spring the tape had

softened, but the words remained legible.

One rainy afternoon the college student stepped off a train

and saw the familiar blue canopy above a stranger's head.

She started to call out. Then she noticed the tape and the

stranger holding the umbrella over a woman with a

stroller. She kept walking through the rain to the bus

shelter.

The umbrella had not returned to her. It had gone farther

than she would have carried it. She smiled at the thought

that forgetting something had given it a job.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

5

3. A Recipe with No Measurements

Nina asked her grandmother for the recipe to the soup

that appeared whenever anyone in the family was sick.

Her grandmother said, "An onion, if you have one. A

handful of rice. Enough water." Nina brought a notebook

and demanded amounts.

They cooked together. The grandmother stopped to taste

the broth four times. When Nina tried to write "four

tastes," she laughed. "That isn't an ingredient."

Years later Nina lived three states away. Her grandmother

could no longer stand long enough to cook, so Nina made

the soup and brought it over. It was too salty. Nina

apologized. Her grandmother ate a whole bowl.

"You used too little water," she said. "Next time you'll

know."

Nina opened her old notebook. On the recipe page she had

written a dozen numbers and, at the bottom, one sentence

she had nearly forgotten: Sit down while it simmers. She

pulled out a chair. The soup cooled a little. They talked

about the year her grandmother had learned to drive, and

nobody mentioned the salt again.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

6

4. The Bus Stop Library

A little wooden box appeared beside the bus stop with a

sign: TAKE A BOOK, LEAVE A BOOK. On the first day it

held five mysteries and a manual for an outdated printer.

By the end of the week the mysteries were gone. The

printer manual remained.

Mr. Alvarez, who caught the seven-fifteen bus, began

keeping a list of what passed through. A cookbook, a

comic, a book of poems with a coffee stain. He liked

imagining the readers, though he did not know most of

their names.

One morning he found a note tucked inside the printer

manual: Page 42 fixed my old machine. Thank you to

whoever left this. Someone had finally taken the least

promising book in the box.

He replaced it with a guide to repairing bicycles. The next

week another note appeared: My daughter's bike rides

again. Mr. Alvarez started putting practical books on the

bottom shelf. The mysteries still traveled faster, but he no

longer called the slow books failures. Sometimes the right

reader needed time to arrive.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

7

5. The Wrong Number

"Is this the bakery?" a woman asked when Marcus

answered his phone. He told her she had the wrong

number. She apologized and hung up. Ten minutes later

she called again, flustered, and read the number aloud.

One digit had been copied incorrectly on a flyer.

Marcus found the bakery's number online and gave it to

her. "I need a cake by tomorrow," she explained. "My

father is turning eighty, and I forgot to order."

The bakery was closed. Marcus thought of the lemon cake

cooling on his counter, made for a meeting that had been

canceled. He did not offer it; a stranger's birthday was

more complicated than a spare dessert. Instead he called a

nearby grocery with a late bakery counter and checked

what they had. Then he called her back.

"You didn't have to do that," she said.

"I know. Tell him happy birthday."

The next evening a message arrived from an unknown

number: a photograph of an older man grinning over a

cake with uneven blue letters. Marcus had never met him.

For a moment, it felt as though he had been invited to the

party.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

8

6. Sunday Shoes

Leah's son announced he would not wear the polished

shoes she had set beside his church clothes. They pinched.

She told him they had fit last month. He answered that his

feet had changed since last month.

On the drive, Leah remembered how many times adults

had told her to be grateful for things that hurt. She turned

the car around. Her son expected a lecture. Instead she

asked him to bring his comfortable sneakers.

At church an older woman smiled at his bright green laces.

"Those look ready for a long day," she said. He smiled back

and sang louder than usual.

That afternoon Leah put the polished shoes in a bag for a

younger cousin, with a note that they should be tried on

before anyone promised to wear them. She was not proud

of having argued over shoes. She was glad she had

changed her mind before the day was over.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

9

7. The Porch Light

After her husband died, Elise kept the porch light on until

midnight. Their house stood at the end of a dark lane. She

told herself it was for deliveries, though none came after

sunset. Really she had grown used to leaving a light for

someone coming home.

In October a teenager from two doors down knocked to

ask if he could sit on her steps until his mother finished a

late shift. He had forgotten his key. Elise brought him a

blanket and cocoa. He came back once more, this time

with permission and a spare key, just to show her he had

remembered it.

By winter neighbors used Elise's porch as a meeting place

before evening walks. Some nights she joined them. Some

nights she waved through the window. The light still

burned until midnight.

It did not mean she expected her husband to return. It

meant the lane had a place where people could see the

path.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

10

8. A Small Applause

At the school talent show, eight-year-old Mina forgot the

second verse of her song. She stood beneath the hot lights

and stared at the microphone. Someone in the front row

began clapping a slow beat. Her teacher joined in. Soon

the room was keeping time together.

Mina could not recall the words. She hummed the melody

to the end and walked offstage. She cried behind the

curtain because she believed humming was a failure.

Her teacher waited until the room was quiet. "You found a

way to finish," she said. "That is a skill."

The next year Mina returned with the same song, lyrics

written on a card in her pocket. She sang both verses. The

audience applauded at the end, but the sound she

remembered most was the patient beat from the year

before, when nobody had demanded she be perfect to stay

on the stage.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

11

9. The Last Tomato

Two neighbors grew tomatoes in pots on opposite sides of

a shared fence. Each believed the other's plants looked

healthier. At summer's end one red tomato remained on

each vine. Mrs. Cho picked hers and set it on Mr. Price's

step because he had been ill. Mr. Price, recovered enough

to walk outside, picked his and placed it on Mrs. Cho's

step because her granddaughter was visiting.

At noon they met at the fence, each holding the other's

tomato and looking embarrassed. The granddaughter

proposed sandwiches. Mrs. Cho supplied bread; Mr. Price

supplied cheese. They sliced both tomatoes and ate at a

small table in the shade.

No one could say whose harvest had been better. The last

fruit of the season had become lunch for three, which was

more than either plant could have managed alone.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

12

10. The Red Scarf

A red scarf hung on the coat rack at the community center

for weeks. Nobody claimed it. When the heater broke

during a winter meeting, the coordinator wrapped it

around a shivering visitor. The visitor left it neatly folded.

The next day a dance instructor borrowed it for a child

waiting for a ride.

In March a woman came to ask for the scarf. Her sister

had knitted it before moving overseas. The coordinator

apologized for its travels and offered to have it cleaned.

The woman ran a finger over a loose stitch.

"My sister did that," she said. "She always rushed the last

row."

The coordinator explained where the scarf had been. The

woman listened, then laughed softly. "That sounds like her

too." She took it home, washed it, and wore it to meet her

sister at the airport. The loose stitch was still there.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

13

11. The Birthday Cake

Darren had no money for the decorated cake his daughter

had circled in a store advertisement. He baked one from a

box mix after she went to sleep. The top sank. The icing

tore crumbs from the sides. He arranged strawberries

around the dent and put a candle in the middle.

At breakfast his daughter saw it and shouted, "It's a

volcano!" She asked for red jam to make lava. Together

they poured it down the sides. By party time the cake

looked like an eruption planned by two very enthusiastic

scientists.

Years later she kept a photograph of it in her apartment.

The expensive cakes from other birthdays had been

delicious, but she could not remember their decorations.

She remembered her father laughing in the kitchen while

they made a mistake look intentional. It had tasted of

strawberries and chocolate and the relief of being allowed

to improvise.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

14

12. The Name Tag

On her first day at the clinic, the receptionist printed a

name tag for Ruth with the wrong name. Ruth had

corrected people so often that she almost let it go. She was

new, and she wanted to be easy to work with.

A nurse noticed her hesitation. "Is that right?" she asked.

Ruth shook her head. The nurse printed another tag, then

walked her through the building and introduced her

properly at every door.

It took less than five minutes. At lunch Ruth thanked her.

"People usually tell me it doesn't matter."

"Then they can wear somebody else's name for a day," the

nurse said.

Ruth kept the correct tag long after she learned everyone

at the clinic. Its plastic clip had a crack, and the lettering

began to fade. She liked the small proof that she had

asked to be seen clearly, and someone had listened

without making the request seem large.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

15

13. Twenty Minutes

A father promised his daughter twenty minutes of

undivided attention after dinner. The first evening they

built a paper bridge. The second they argued over the

rules of a card game. The third he was tired and asked to

postpone it. She said okay, but she set the cards on the

table anyway.

He came back from washing dishes and sat down. The

game lasted eleven minutes. For the remaining nine they

talked about a classmate who had stopped sitting with her

at lunch. He could not solve the problem. He asked

questions and listened.

The next week she set a timer herself. Some nights twenty

minutes became forty. Some stayed twenty. The number

was not magic. It was small enough to promise honestly

and long enough for a quiet thing to find its way into

words.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

16

14. The Quilt Square

After Aunt June died, her nieces found a box of unfinished

quilt squares. Each had a pencil mark on the back: a date,

a place, sometimes a person's name. One square carried

the year she first voted. Another bore the name of a friend

who had taught her to drive. A third was marked simply

the day I came home.

The nieces argued about finishing the quilt. Neither knew

June's pattern. Their uncle said she changed patterns

whenever she learned a better one. They laid the squares

on the floor and arranged them by color, then by date,

then by what felt right.

The finished quilt had a crooked corner. They kept it.

When family visited, someone always asked about a

square, and another person remembered a piece of the

story. June had not left a perfect map of her life. She had

left enough cloth for the family to keep talking.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

17

15. A Seat by the Window

At the hospital, Mr. Finch always asked for the chair by

the window. His daughter thought he wanted a view of the

parking lot. One afternoon she arrived early and found him

watching a worker water the small trees along the curb.

"He does it even when it rains," Mr. Finch said. "He checks

the roots first."

The worker had become part of his daily clock: trees at

nine, mail cart at ten, lunch at noon. When Mr. Finch went

home, his daughter bought a small tree for his yard. They

planted it together, slowly, with breaks for tea.

He did not recover all at once. Each morning he looked out

and checked the soil. The tree grew a little. The routine

gave him something to care for while he learned again

how to accept being cared for.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

18

16. The Pencil Box

Sam found an old pencil box while cleaning the classroom.

Inside were three short pencils, a marble, and a note that

said, You can sit with us tomorrow. No name was signed.

He showed it to his teacher, who remembered the box

belonging to a child who had moved away years before.

They left it on a shelf rather than throw it out. That

autumn a new student arrived and spent her first lunch

alone. Sam thought of the note. He wrote the same words

on clean paper, signed his name, and carried it to her

desk.

She joined his table the next day. The pencil box did not

make him kind. It reminded him that someone once had

been, and that a small invitation could outlast the day it

was written.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

19

17. Three Good Things

On a hard evening, Imani's mother suggested that they

name three good things before bed. Imani disliked the

idea. Her exam had gone badly, the bus was late, and a

friend had canceled their plans. "I only have one," she

said. "The dog didn't eat my homework."

Her mother counted it. After a while Imani added that the

bus driver had waited while an older passenger found her

seat. Then she remembered the warm bread at dinner.

None of it fixed the exam or the friendship.

They kept the practice without making it a rule. Some

nights they named three. Some nights they could barely

find one. Her mother never told her that good things

canceled bad ones. They wrote both kinds of day in the

same notebook and turned the page when they were

ready.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

20

18. The Garden Gate

Mr. Okafor planted flowers beside the gate between his

yard and the apartment path. Children stopped to touch

the petals. He worried they would break the stems, so he

put up a sign asking them to look with their eyes. The next

morning a child had drawn a careful picture of the flowers

and taped it below his sign.

He added a second sign: Ask me if you want to help water

them. On Saturday three children appeared with plastic

cups. They spilled most of the water on their shoes. He

showed them how to pour near the roots. By summer each

child knew which blooms opened first.

The gate stayed latched, but the garden no longer felt like

a border. Mr. Okafor still corrected careless hands. He

also learned the names of the hands that came back to

help.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

21

19. A Cup of Tea

At the laundromat, two women reached for the same last

chair. One was carrying a baby. The other had spent the

day standing at work. They looked at each other and both

stepped back.

The owner brought a second chair from the office. While

the dryers turned, he made tea in paper cups for all three

of them. They talked about detergent, then children, then

how difficult it was to ask for a place to rest.

The baby fell asleep. When the laundry was done, the

women folded their clothes together so neither had to hold

a basket and a child at once. The owner put the chairs side

by side for the next customers. It was a small change in a

room where people had often competed for a single seat.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

22

20. The Missing Button

A man came to Mara's alterations counter with a coat

missing one button. He needed it for an interview in an

hour. None of the spare buttons matched. Mara proposed

replacing all four with plain dark ones. He watched the

clock while she worked.

"Is this job important?" she asked.

"Very," he said. "But I'm trying to remember it won't

decide my whole life."

She finished with ten minutes to spare. He paid and left,

then returned just long enough to say he had forgotten to

thank her. Months later he stopped by wearing the same

coat. He had not gotten that job. He had found another,

one he liked better. The buttons were still secure.

Mara had kept the original three in an envelope in case he

wanted them back. He told her to keep them. "They don't

match where I'm going," he said.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

23

21. The Long Way Home

Every day after school, Ben took the long route past the

fire station. His mother thought he liked the trucks. In

fact, he liked the station dog, who waited by the fence and

wagged at everyone. When the dog was absent for a week,

Ben worried but did not know whom to ask.

A firefighter noticed him lingering and explained that the

old dog was recovering from surgery. Ben drew a card

with a crooked red engine and wrote Get well, Captain.

The firefighters hung it above the dog's bed.

The next week Captain returned to the fence, moving

slowly. Ben waved. The firefighter who had spoken to him

waved too. It was still the long way home, but now he

knew the names of some of the people along it.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

24

22. The Paper Star

On a night shift at the grocery, Celia folded a star from a

receipt while the registers were quiet. She had learned to

do it as a child. A coworker asked for one, then another for

his daughter. Soon a row of tiny stars sat above the break

room sink.

A manager said they made the room look untidy. Celia

took them down. At the end of the week he returned one

star to the shelf. His son had been in the hospital, he

explained, and the coworker had brought him the little

folded shape. He carried it in his pocket through a long

afternoon.

They kept the stars on a corkboard after that, away from

the sink. No one pretended paper could cure an illness. It

could say, without taking much space, that someone had

thought of you while folding each point.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

25

23. The Little Choir

The community choir had twelve members and one person

who could not reliably sing the melody. Mrs. Avery came

every Tuesday and sang a harmony no one had written.

Some members wanted the director to ask her to listen

instead. The director asked Mrs. Avery to stand beside him

for rehearsal.

He learned that she could hear lower notes more clearly

than high ones. He changed her part. The harmony she

had been chasing settled into place, and the whole group

sounded fuller.

At the concert, a microphone failed. Mrs. Avery's strong

lower voice carried the opening line until the technician

fixed it. Afterward she thanked the director for being

patient. He said he should have listened sooner. They both

meant it.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

26

24. The Snow Shovel

The first snow of the year covered three front walks on

Willow Street. A teenager cleared her grandmother's

steps, then kept going to the next house because the

shovel was already in her hands. She stopped after the

third house, tired and late for lunch.

By evening someone had cleared the path to her

grandmother's mailbox. She never found out who. In the

morning a narrow trail led from one end of the street to

the other. Different shovels had left different marks, and

no one had organized a thing.

The teenager took a photograph before new snow softened

the lines. It looked like a map made by people who each

knew only the next few feet.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

27

25. The Second Drawing

When Rosa's father saw her drawing of their house, he

praised the straight lines. She hid the other drawing

beneath it. In that one the house floated in a purple sky,

and the front door was shaped like a mouth. She had

worked longer on it, but she expected him to ask why a

house looked so strange.

He found it while clearing the table. "Tell me about this

door," he said. Rosa explained that houses listened, but

hers should be able to speak when someone was lonely. He

put the two drawings side by side on the refrigerator.

A week later he drew a tiny speech bubble next to the

door: Come in. Rosa added a second one: There's room.

Neither drawing had straight lines by then.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

28

26. The Lemon Tree

A lemon tree stood on the apartment balcony long after its

owner moved away. The new tenant, Harper, inherited it

with yellowing leaves and no instructions. She watered it

too much. A neighbor downstairs called up, "Try less. It

likes to dry a little."

He had helped the former tenant carry the tree up three

flights years before. He knew which side of the balcony got

morning light. Harper moved the pot and followed his

advice. In spring it bloomed.

The first lemon was small and oddly shaped. Harper cut it

in half, made two glasses of lemonade, and took one

downstairs. The neighbor drank it without commenting on

the sourness. They both looked up at the balcony, where

another flower had opened.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

29

27. The Interview Suit

A career center kept a rack of donated suits for people

attending interviews. One jacket had a tiny stitched heart

inside the collar. Malik chose it because it fit his

shoulders. On the bus he noticed the stitch and wondered

who had worn it first.

He did not get the job. Back at the center he brushed the

jacket and returned it. The volunteer asked whether he

wanted to reserve it for another interview. He said yes.

Three interviews later, an employer offered him a position.

Malik bought his own jacket when he could afford one. He

donated a pair of sturdy shoes to the rack and added a

small note inside: You deserve to walk in comfortably. He

never learned who had sewn the heart. Someone else

would find both gifts in their own time.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

30

28. A Letter in the Drawer

After moving, Ada found a letter she had written to her

younger self for a school assignment. She had promised to

become a famous pianist and never make a mistake in

public. She was now a librarian who played at home with

the window open.

For a moment she felt she had disappointed the girl who

wrote it. Then she remembered the child had been afraid

of a recital. "Never make a mistake" had been less a dream

than a plea.

Ada wrote a reply and put both letters in the drawer. She

told her younger self about the library children who asked

for another song after story time, even when she missed a

note. She told her that a life could change direction

without becoming smaller. The next evening she played

with the window open again.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

31

29. The Dance Lesson

At seventy-two, Walter signed up for a beginner dance

class. He arrived early and stood near the door, ready to

leave if everyone else was twenty. The first person to greet

him was an eighty-year-old woman who had taken the

course three times.

"Do you know the steps?" he asked.

"Some of them," she said. "I come because I like the

music."

Walter stepped on her shoe during the first lesson. She

stepped on his during the second. By the fourth they could

cross the room without apologizing. He had expected to

become a dancer or discover he could not. Instead he had

found an hour each week when learning something badly

was allowed to be fun.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

32

30. The Open Door

During a neighborhood power outage, Priya opened her

front door because her hallway held the only battery

lantern she could find. A neighbor saw the light and came

to check on her. Another arrived with candles. Soon five

people sat on the floor sharing crackers and stories about

the loud storm outside.

When the electricity returned, nobody stood up

immediately. Priya had lived there for two years and

known only one neighbor's name. By the time the lantern

went off, she knew four more.

The next week she invited them for dinner while the lights

were working. They sat at a table this time. The door had

first opened for practical reasons; it stayed open because

people remembered how easily they had found one

another.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

33

31. The Quiet Victory

After six weeks of practice, Jo made a phone call she had

been avoiding. She arranged an appointment, wrote down

the time, and hung up. No one else knew what it had cost

her to dial. She nearly told her sister and then decided it

was too small to explain.

At dinner her sister asked how the day had gone. Jo said,

"I did a hard thing." Her sister lifted her water glass in a

toast without asking for details. Jo lifted hers too.

Later she shared the story. Her sister admitted she had

spent that same afternoon asking for help with a problem

she had hidden for months. They toasted again, this time

to two quiet victories. The glasses made an ordinary little

sound. It was enough.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

34

32. The Orange in the Lunchbox

Each day Alina's father peeled an orange for her lunch and

packed the pieces in a small container. At thirteen she

asked him to stop. She was old enough to peel her own. He

put a whole orange in the lunchbox the next morning and

did not argue.

At school she struggled with the thick skin and sprayed

juice on a worksheet. Her friends laughed kindly. She

laughed too. That evening she asked her father how he

managed to keep the pieces neat. He showed her the first

small cut he made near the stem.

For a while they alternated. Some days he peeled it; some

days she did. When she left for college, he packed an

orange in the car. She peeled it at a rest stop, made the

small cut correctly, and called to tell him. He asked if the

fruit was sweet. She said it was.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

35

33. The Saturday Call

Two brothers called each other every Saturday. At first the

calls were long, full of plans and advice. As they grew

older, some lasted only five minutes. They discussed

weather, a leaking faucet, the score of a game neither had

watched.

One Saturday the younger brother was too tired to talk.

The older said, "That's fine. I'll stay on while you make

coffee." They listened to the kettle and the clink of a

spoon. After a few minutes the younger brother told him

what had really been wrong.

Neither could fix it before lunch. They made a plan to meet

the next week. The call ended with the ordinary question,

"Same time Saturday?" It had become their way of saying

they would keep a place in the week for each other.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

36

34. The Map of Home

A teacher asked her students to draw a map of home.

Some drew houses; one drew an apartment building;

another drew a bus route between two homes. Eli drew

the basketball court behind the library and the bench

where his grandfather waited during games.

He worried that he had misunderstood. His teacher asked

him to explain the landmarks. He pointed to the place

where he had learned to dribble and the corner where his

grandfather always waved. She pinned the map beside the

others.

At pickup, his grandfather studied it for a long time. "You

left out the snack shop," he said with mock seriousness. Eli

added a square for it in green marker. The court and the

bench stayed at the center. He had drawn the place where

somebody was always glad to see him.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

37

35. The Soup Pot

At the end of a busy winter, the community kitchen had

carrots, rice, beans, and three kinds of broth left over from

different meals. The cook made soup. It was not on the

menu, and no two bowls looked exactly alike. She set it out

with bread and a sign that said, Come as you are. It is

warm.

A woman in a work uniform ate beside a retired mechanic.

Two children compared which bowl had more carrots. A

man who usually took his food to go stayed to wash dishes.

Nobody asked for the recipe, because there was no way to

make the same soup again. The ingredients had come from

a particular week and a particular set of hands.

The cook cleaned the empty pot at closing. She liked

knowing it was empty. In the morning she would begin

with whatever the day brought, and there would be room

for someone to sit down.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

38

36. The Grocery List

When Dad began forgetting small things, he wrote grocery

lists in block letters and taped them to the refrigerator.

Sometimes the lists included milk twice. Sometimes they

ended with a word no one could decipher. His daughter

offered to take over the shopping, but he liked choosing

the apples himself.

They made a new list together. She drew little boxes

beside each item. At the store he checked them off slowly,

then added a chocolate bar at the bottom in his own hand.

"For the driver," he said. She was driving.

The next week she found the old lists in a drawer. She kept

one that read milk, bread, apples, call June. The last item

was not groceries. It was what he wanted to remember

after they got home. She called her aunt while he put the

apples in a bowl.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

39

37. The Spare Key

A woman gave her neighbor a spare key before a long trip.

The neighbor promised to water the plants and bring in

the mail. When the woman returned, her kitchen table

held a note: The fern is stubborn. I tried. The fern looked

healthier than it had in months.

The key stayed with the neighbor. Later it let a plumber in

during a leak, and once it rescued a guest who had locked

her phone inside. One evening the neighbor used it only to

put a warm loaf on the table while the woman was working

late.

They agreed the key could be returned whenever either

felt uncomfortable. Neither did. It was a small piece of

metal that opened one door, and a larger sign that trust

was something they kept checking and renewing.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

40

38. The Rained-Out Picnic

A family planned a picnic for weeks. At the park, rain came

down before anyone could open the basket. They drove

home disappointed, carrying soggy napkins and a blanket

that smelled of wet grass.

The youngest child suggested spreading the blanket on the

living room floor. Her brother built a cardboard sun and

taped it to the lamp. Their mother served sandwiches from

the cooler. Their father played bird calls on his phone until

everyone asked him to stop.

The rain lasted all afternoon. They ate under a paper sun

and opened the windows to hear it. On the next clear

weekend they returned to the park. The family enjoyed the

real trees, but the children asked whether they could have

another indoor picnic when the weather turned bad. A

spoiled plan had become a second tradition.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

41

39. The Repair Jar

In the school workshop, a teacher kept a glass jar labeled

REPAIRS. Students dropped in loose screws, bent clips,

and buttons found on the floor. Once a week they sorted

the pieces and fixed what they could: a wobbly chair, a

lunchbox latch, a drawer that would not close.

A student named Devon brought in a small radio that had

belonged to his grandfather. He was afraid to touch it. The

teacher did not promise they could repair it. They opened

the case together and found a broken wire. Devon

soldered it while the teacher watched. The radio crackled,

then played a song.

He took it home and gave it to his grandfather, who turned

the dial with shaking fingers. The jar never held

everything that needed mending. It held enough to let

people begin.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

42

40. The Library Card

When Mrs. Reed retired, she got her first library card in

forty years. She had spent so long buying books for her

classroom that borrowing one for herself felt almost

extravagant. The librarian asked what she liked. Mrs.

Reed said she did not know anymore.

They started with a mystery, a gardening book, and a

novel set by the sea. She returned the mystery half read

and apologized. The librarian said returning a book

unfinished was allowed. Mrs. Reed took a book of travel

essays instead.

By summer she had a list of authors she loved and a longer

list she did not. The card did not tell her who she was now.

It gave her permission to find out without paying for every

wrong guess.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

43

41. The Green Bench

A city worker painted a park bench green. Before the paint

dried, someone carved a small heart into one corner. He

sighed, sanded the mark, and painted over it. The next

week a woman asked why the heart was gone. Her late

husband had carved it years earlier, she said, before the

bench was replaced.

The worker had not known. He offered to carve a new

heart with her watching, then hesitated. "Would that feel

false?" he asked.

She thought about it. They chose a small brass plaque

instead, with her husband's name and the words He

always saved me this seat. She sat there after he installed

it. The new bench could not become the old one, but it

could carry part of the story forward.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

44

42. The First Stitch

At a sewing circle, a teenager brought a torn backpack

and said she had never held a needle. The others showed

her how to thread it, knot it, and pull the needle through

without catching the lining. Her first stitches wandered

across the fabric.

She wanted to take them out. The woman beside her said

the seam was strong and asked whether the backpack had

to look new. It did not. It had to last through the rest of the

school year.

The teenager finished the repair and added a bright patch

over the tear. Her next stitches were straighter. She kept

the first crooked row underneath. It reminded her that a

beginning could hold even when it was not pretty.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

45

43. The Thank-You Note

A school custodian found a note taped to his supply cart:

Thank you for finding my lost bracelet. He had not found a

bracelet. He asked around until he learned another

custodian on the evening shift had found it and left it at

the office.

He moved the note to the right cart and added a line of his

own: You made somebody's day. The evening custodian

read it after most students had gone home. She had

thought of the bracelet as one more item on a long list of

things to return.

The next week she left a note for the morning shift about a

classroom window that would not close. Beneath it she

wrote, Thanks for starting the day before I get here. The

cart became a place for useful messages and occasional

kindness.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

46

44. The Roadside Flowers

A woman stopped beside a country road to photograph

wildflowers. A driver pulled over to check whether her car

had broken down. She thanked him and showed him the

patch of yellow blossoms. He had passed it every day for

years without noticing.

The following week he took the same road with his

granddaughter. He pointed out the flowers, then the old

stone wall behind them. She asked who had built the wall.

He did not know. They went to the local history room on

Saturday and found a photograph of the field from eighty

years before.

The flowers had brought him to the wall; the wall brought

them to a story. On the way home his granddaughter

pointed out a stand of blue blooms neither of them had

seen that morning. They stopped again.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

47

45. The Last Page

Amara's mother had read aloud to her when she was

young, stopping at the most exciting moment with a grin.

Years later Amara visited during her mother's recovery

from surgery and brought a novel they had both meant to

read. This time Amara read the chapters.

Her mother fell asleep before the ending. Amara placed a

bookmark where she had stopped. The next afternoon they

read the final pages together. It was a sad ending, and

neither of them liked it much. They spent an hour

imagining a better one.

When Amara packed to leave, her mother asked her to

keep the book. Amara tucked it in her bag with the

bookmark still inside. The ending on the printed page

would not change. Their conversation about it was the part

she wanted to carry home.

A PLACE AT THE TABLE

48

Afterword

A warm story cannot promise that every problem will be

solved. These stories make a smaller promise: a person

can be noticed, helped, heard, or invited in. Sometimes the

gesture changes a whole life. Sometimes it changes an

afternoon. Both are worth remembering.

title: Coding Classroom Lessons 1 to 5 — Step-by-step
content:
S3LFM@DE Solutions Coding Classroom Lessons 1 to 5

A hands-on return to coding for Templar Hughes-Bryant. Work through these five short lessons in order. Each one explains a concept, gives you code to type, and ends with a small change to make yourself. Save your practice in a folder named Coding Classroom. You can use a free text editor and open each HTML file by double-clicking it.

Detailed step format used in this revision

• Every action is kept in the original order.

• Complete one numbered action at a time. Do not jump ahead.

• For each action, the added click-by-click breakdown tells you what to click, what to type, and what to check.

• After changing a file, press Ctrl+S unless the lesson specifically tells you not to save yet.

• If your screen does not match the written checkpoint, stop on that step and correct it before continuing.

Getting started

Create a folder named Coding Classroom on your computer. Inside it, create index.html. On Windows, turn on File name extensions in File Explorer so the file does not accidentally become index.html.txt. Open it in your editor, then open it in a browser to see the result. After edits, save and refresh the browser.

Lesson 1 How a web page is built

HTML provides structure. A browser reads elements such as headings and paragraphs, then displays them. The opening and closing tags mark what each element contains.

Type this

<!doctype html>

<html lang="en">

<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>My Practice Page</title></head>

<body>

<h1>S3LFM@DE Solutions</h1>

<p>Let’s bring your vision to life.</p>

</body>

</html>

Your turn

Change the heading to your own name. Add a second paragraph about a service you enjoy offering.

Check yourself

What does the title tag change? Why is the h1 visible on the page?

Answer: The title appears in the browser tab; h1 is a visible heading in the body.

My notes: __________________________________________________________________

___________________________________________________________________________

Lesson 2 Links images and useful sections

A link uses an anchor element and an href destination. Images use src and descriptive alt text. Sections group related content. Keep contact details accurate when working on a real site.

Type this

<section>

<h2>About the founder</h2>

<p>Templar Hughes-Bryant is the founder and CEO.</p>

<a href="https://example.com">Visit a sample link</a>

<img src="portrait.jpg" alt="Portrait of the founder" width="220">

</section>

Your turn

Add this section inside body. Replace portrait.jpg only if you have an image in the same folder. Add a Services section with a short list of three services.

Check yourself

What happens if portrait.jpg is missing? What does alt text do?

Answer: The image cannot load; alt text describes it to assistive technology and may appear when loading fails.

My notes: __________________________________________________________________

___________________________________________________________________________

Lesson 3 Make it look like yours with CSS

CSS styles the HTML. A selector chooses elements; declarations set properties. Place a style element inside head for this exercise.

Type this

<style>

body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background: #101827; color: #fff; margin: 40px; }

h1 { color: #d9ad5b; }

section { border: 1px solid #d9ad5b; padding: 20px; border-radius: 12px; }

a { color: #f4d594; }

</style>

Your turn

Add the style block to your HTML head. Try a different background color and increase the section padding to 28px. Refresh after saving.

Check yourself

Which rule changes text color for the whole page? What is padding?

Answer: The body color rule sets inherited text color; padding adds space inside an element.

My notes: __________________________________________________________________

___________________________________________________________________________

Lesson 4 Add a button that works

JavaScript can respond to a click. Give an element an id, find it with document.getElementById, and attach a click handler. Put the script just before the closing body tag.

Type this

<button id="helloButton">Say hello</button>

<p id="message"></p>

<script>

const button = document.getElementById("helloButton");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {

document.getElementById("message").textContent = "You built this, Templar!";

});

</script>

Your turn

Add the button, paragraph, and script. Click the button. Change the message to a greeting for a visitor.

Check yourself

Why must the id in JavaScript match the HTML id exactly?

Answer: The browser uses that string to find the element. A mismatch returns null and the click handler cannot be attached.

My notes: __________________________________________________________________

___________________________________________________________________________

Lesson 5 Practice a tiny quote calculator

A function can turn inputs into an output. Here the visitor enters a quantity, then the page multiplies it by a sample $75 flyer price. This is a practice calculator, not a live ordering system.

Type this

<label for="quantity">Flyer quantity</label>

<input id="quantity" type="number" min="1" value="1">

<button id="calculate">Calculate</button>

<p id="result"></p>

<script>

document.getElementById("calculate").addEventListener("click", function () {

const quantity = Number(document.getElementById("quantity").value);

const result = document.getElementById("result");

if (!Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1) {

result.textContent = "Enter a whole number of at least 1.";

return;

}

result.textContent = "Practice total: $" + (quantity * 75).toFixed(2);

});

</script>

Your turn

Use this on a fresh practice page or replace the Lesson 4 script to avoid duplicate IDs. Try quantities 1 and 3, then try 0. Change the sample price to 85 and test again.

Check yourself

What does Number() do? Why check for a positive whole number?

Answer: Number() converts input text into a number. Validation prevents invalid quantities from producing misleading totals.

My notes: __________________________________________________________________

___________________________________________________________________________

title: Coding Classroom Lessons 6 to 20 — Step-by-step
content:
S3LFM@DE Solutions Coding Classroom Lessons 6 to 20

This completes the 20 lesson classroom. You will build a local practice version of a business site, then learn how to check, publish, and maintain it. Follow each numbered action in order. Your production customer and admin portals, accounts, and Stripe payments require a separate backend and secure configuration; these lessons do not replace those systems.

Detailed step format used in this revision

• Every action is kept in the original order.

• Complete one numbered action at a time. Do not jump ahead.

• For each action, the added click-by-click breakdown tells you what to click, what to type, and what to check.

• After changing a file, press Ctrl+S unless the lesson specifically tells you not to save yet.

• If your screen does not match the written checkpoint, stop on that step and correct it before continuing.

Before Lesson 6

Finish Lessons 1 to 5. In your Coding Classroom folder, make a new folder called site-practice. Make three empty files in it: index.html, style.css, and script.js. In Windows File Explorer, turn on View > Show > File name extensions. Open the folder in your editor. The address for local practice will begin with file:/// when you double-click index.html.

Your final folder

site-practice/

index.html

style.css

script.js

images/

founder.jpg (only if you choose to add your own photo)

Type the code yourself if you want the practice. You can copy it when your hand needs a break. Save after every change, then refresh the browser. Use the sample content here for practice; check your live site before making any real update.

Lesson 6 Build the page foundation

File: index.html

Where and what to change

Replace the entire contents of index.html with this starting page. Keep the three file names exactly as shown.

Type this

<!doctype html>

<html lang="en">

<head>

<meta charset="utf-8">

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

<title>S3LFM@DE Solutions Practice</title>

<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">

<script src="script.js" defer></script>

</head>

<body>

<header class="site-header">

<a class="brand" href="#home">S3LFM@DE Solutions</a>

<nav aria-label="Main navigation">

<a href="#about">About</a>

<a href="#services">Services</a>

<a href="#contact">Contact</a>

</nav>

</header>

<main id="home">

<section class="hero">

<h1>Let’s bring your vision to life.</h1>

<p>Creative and practical support for people and businesses.</p>

<a class="button" href="#services">Explore services</a>

</section>

</main>

<footer><p>© <span id="year"></span> S3LFM@DE Solutions</p></footer>

</body>

</html>

Save and check

Save index.html and double-click it. A plain heading, links, and footer should appear. The year is empty until Lesson 12.

If it does not work

If you see raw tags, confirm the extension is .html. If the page is blank, confirm you saved the file and reopen it.

My notes: _______________________________________________________________

Lesson 7 Connect the visual design

File: style.css

Where and what to change

Put this complete starting stylesheet in style.css. It is linked from the head of index.html.

Type this

* { box-sizing: border-box; }

html { scroll-behavior: smooth; }

body { margin: 0; font: 16px/1.6 Arial, sans-serif; color: #f8f4e9; background: #111827; }

a { color: inherit; }

.site-header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 20px; padding: 18px 5%; background: #10121b; }

.brand { font-weight: bold; color: #dfb65d; text-decoration: none; }

nav { display: flex; gap: 18px; flex-wrap: wrap; }

nav a { text-decoration: none; }

.hero { padding: 100px 6%; text-align: center; background: linear-gradient(135deg,#111827,#382c46); }

h1 { font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 5vw, 4rem); line-height: 1.1; }

.button, button { display: inline-block; background: #dfb65d; color: #17131b; border: 0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 12px 20px; font-weight: bold; text-decoration: none; cursor: pointer; }

section:not(.hero) { padding: 64px 6%; }

footer { padding: 22px 6%; text-align: center; background: #0c1018; }

Save and check

Save style.css and refresh index.html. The page should be navy and gold with a large hero.

If it does not work

If nothing changes, check that style.css is beside index.html and that the link spelling matches.

My notes: _______________________________________________________________

Lesson 8 Add the founder story

File: index.html

Where and what to change

Inside main, after the closing tag of the hero section and before </main>, paste this section.

Type this

<section id="about" aria-labelledby="about-title">

<div class="content">

<h2 id="about-title">Meet the founder</h2>

<p><strong>Templar Hughes-Bryant, Founder and CEO</strong></p>

<p>I believe thoughtful work can help turn an idea into something people can use and remember.</p>

</div>

</section>

Save and check

Save and refresh. Click About in the navigation; it should jump to the new section. Rewrite the sample bio in your own words.

If it does not work

If the link does not jump, compare href="#about" to id="about" letter for letter.

My notes: _______________________________________________________________

Lesson 9 Add all service categories

File: index.html

Where and what to change

Add this section after About, still inside main. The categories are your current site categories; this is a classroom copy, so verify wording against the live version before publishing.

Type this

<section id="services" aria-labelledby="services-title">

<h2 id="services-title">Services</h2>

<div class="service-grid">

<article><h3>Website Design</h3><p>Sites and page updates.</p></article>

<article><h3>Branding & Creative</h3><p>Visual materials and ideas.</p></article>

<article><h3>Business Tools</h3><p>Practical tools and templates.</p></article>

<article><h3>Career & Office</h3><p>Resumes and office support.</p></article>

<article><h3>Research & Writing</h3><p>Clear, useful writing.</p></article>

<article><h3>Clerical Support</h3><p>Organized administrative work.</p></article>

<article><h3>Event Planning</h3><p>Materials and planning support.</p></article>

<article><h3>Social Media & Digital Support</h3><p>Digital content support.</p></article>

<article><h3>Business Cards</h3><p>Memorable contact cards.</p></article>

<article><h3>Vocal & Special Occasion Services</h3><p>Creative touches for special moments.</p></article>

</div>

</section>

Save and check

Save and refresh. Count ten cards. Click Services in the navigation.

If it does not work

If an ampersand looks odd, use & in HTML. Do not paste an older six-service section over your real site.

My notes: _______________________________________________________________

Lesson 10 Style the service cards

File: style.css

Where and what to change

Append these rules at the end of style.css.

Type this

.content { max-width: 800px; margin: auto; }

h2 { font-size: clamp(1.8rem, 3vw, 2.6rem); color: #e7c477; }

Client Service Labs Step by Step

S3LFM@DE Solutions | Prepared for Templar Hughes-Bryant

Detailed step format used in this revision

• Every action is kept in the original order.

• Complete one numbered action at a time. Do not jump ahead.

• For each action, the added click-by-click breakdown tells you what to click, what to type, and what to check.

• After changing a file, press Ctrl+S unless the lesson specifically tells you not to save yet.

• If your screen does not match the written checkpoint, stop on that step and correct it before continuing.

Each client project below is divided into separate service jobs. In The Bakery Launch, complete the Website Design job, then the Branding and Creative job, then the Business Tools job, and the remaining jobs for that bakery. The other projects work the same way. You can practice one service without doing the others first, but use the shared client facts so all files agree.

How to complete one service job

1. Read the project’s shared client brief and the source facts.

2. Open the specific service job you want, such as Bakery Launch Website Design.

3. Follow its six steps in order. Each step names the tool, action, and expected file or check.

4. Save the first draft before applying the project’s client change.

5. Run the service job’s final check and keep editable sources and proof copies.

These are fictional exercises. Use placeholder contact information, never invent an unconfirmed client fact, and label any public sample as a concept project. Menu labels can vary by software version.

Service jobs in this workbook

• Project 1 The Bakery Launch: Website Design, Branding and Creative, Business Tools, Social Media and Digital Support, Business Cards.

• Project 2 The Community Event: Event Planning, Clerical Support, Branding and Creative.

• Project 3 The Office Rescue: Business Tools, Career and Office, Clerical Support.

• Project 4 The Job Search Kit: Career and Office, Research and Writing, Business Tools.

• Project 5 The Research Desk: Research and Writing, Business Tools.

• Project 6 The Celebration Plan: Event Planning, Vocal and Special Occasion Services, Branding and Creative.

• Project 7 The Memorial and Community Care Lab: Research and Writing, Clerical Support, Vocal and Special Occasion Services.

• Project 8 The Complete Client Challenge: Website Design, Branding and Creative, Business Tools, Career and Office, Research and Writing, Clerical Support, Event Planning, Social Media and Digital Support, Business Cards, Vocal and Special Occasion Services.

Project 1 The Bakery Launch

Client request: A fictional neighborhood bakery announces that it is opening soon. It does not accept orders or payments yet.

Source facts: Owner Avery Lane. Tuesday–Friday 8 a.m.–2 p.m.; Saturday 8 a.m.–2 p.m. initially. Cinnamon rolls $4, muffins $3, drip coffee $2.50. Address and public contact details are unconfirmed.

Change after draft one: Saturday hours become 9 a.m.–1 p.m. after the first drafts. The address remains unconfirmed.

Fictional client source packet

• Approved short copy: “Fresh bakes for neighborhood mornings.” Status line: “Opening soon. Follow for updates.” No opening date has been approved.

• Menu: cinnamon rolls $4; muffins $3; drip coffee $2.50. Initial hours: Tuesday through Saturday, 8 a.m.–2 p.m. The later revision changes Saturday alone to 9 a.m.–1 p.m.

• Brand direction: warm, simple, neighborhood-friendly. Practice colors may be selected by you; record their exact values. No logo, photographs, address, or public phone number were supplied.

• For practice-only proofs use Avery Lane, Owner, and a placeholder such as avery@morningtable.example. The .example address is fictional and must never be offered as a live way to contact the bakery.

• Five fictional inquiries for the tracker: MT001 Nia Cole asks for opening updates; MT002 Devin Brooks asks about muffins; MT003 Priya Shah asks about hours; MT004 Elias Green asks about coffee; MT005 Tori West asks about accessibility. Use dates October 1 through 5, 2026, in that order. Initial statuses: New, Waiting, New, Closed, New.

• Social topics in order: meet the bakery, cinnamon rolls, menu preview, planned hours, opening updates. The only approved action is “Follow for updates.” No purchasing, reservation, or payment link exists.

• Website pages are Home, Menu, Contact. The Contact page may say “Address and contact details coming soon.” Any contact form is only a mockup unless you build and test a real sending system.

Work one service job at a time. Each job below makes its own deliverable for this same client.

title: Microsoft Office Practice Playground Guidebook
content:
The Microsoft Office Practice Playground Guidebook

Word • Excel • PowerPoint • Access • Plus your PlayLab website

Start Here: The Playground Rule

These files are not client files and they are not your live business website. They exist for one purpose: practice. You are expected to change them, break them, undo changes, rebuild sections, and try ideas that you would never test on a real customer project.

Your practice pack

PlayLab website: HTML/CSS/JavaScript playground with themes, games, notes, cards, and a doodle pad.

Word Practice Lab: Formatting, layouts, tables, business documents, and editing.

Excel Practice Workbook: Formulas, tables, charts, formatting, tracking, invoices, and data cleaning.

PowerPoint Practice Deck: Slide layouts, shapes, typography, charts, images, and presentation flow.

Access Practice Database Kit: A ready-to-import relational practice dataset, SQL queries, and exercises for Microsoft Access.

Part 1 — Microsoft Word

Core skills to learn

Typing and editing; Styles; paragraph spacing; tabs; bullets and numbering; tables; headers and footers; page numbers; sections; images; text wrapping; columns; page breaks; Find/Replace; spellcheck; comments; Track Changes; saving as PDF.

A smart practice routine

Open the Word Practice Lab. Pick one exercise. Save a copy before changing it. Make the change. Undo it. Repeat the change using a different method. This teaches both the feature and the recovery process.

Styles are your secret weapon

Instead of manually making every heading purple, bold, and 18 pt, apply a Heading style. Then change the style definition once. Word updates all matching headings. This is essential for long reports, manuals, proposals, and resumes.

Sections vs. page breaks

A page break simply starts a new page. A section break lets different parts of the same document have different margins, orientation, columns, headers, footers, and page-number rules.

Practice project

Build a 3-page mini business proposal: cover page, services page, pricing table, and contact page. Then make a second version with a completely different visual style.

Part 2 — Microsoft Excel

Excel is easiest when you think in four layers: INPUTS → FORMULAS → SUMMARY → VISUALS.

Data entry

Use one row per record and one column per field. Avoid empty rows inside a dataset. Keep dates as real dates, not text.

Essential formulas

Start with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA, IF, SUMIF/SUMIFS, COUNTIF/COUNTIFS, ROUND, TODAY, TEXT, LEFT/RIGHT/MID, CONCAT/TEXTJOIN, XLOOKUP (or VLOOKUP), and IFERROR.

Relative vs. absolute references

A2 changes when copied. $A$2 stays fixed. A$2 locks only the row. $A2 locks only the column. Practice this until it becomes automatic.

Tables

Turn ranges into Excel Tables. Tables expand automatically, carry formulas downward, filter easily, and make formulas easier to understand.

Conditional formatting

Use it to surface meaning: overdue dates, low inventory, unpaid invoices, high scores, duplicate values, and progress bars.

Charts

Choose charts based on the question: column/bar for comparisons, line for time, pie/doughnut for a small number of parts, scatter for relationships.

Practice project

Build a pretend freelance tracker with client, service, quoted amount, paid amount, due date, status, and balance. Create a dashboard showing total quoted, total paid, outstanding balance, and jobs by status.

Part 3 — Microsoft PowerPoint

Think in slides, not pages

A slide should communicate one main idea. Large text and strong hierarchy matter more than fitting every detail.

Use Slide Master

Put repeating brand elements, fonts, colors, and footer details in the Slide Master so they stay consistent.

Alignment

Use Align and Distribute commands instead of dragging objects by eye. Turn on guides and gridlines when building complex layouts.

Images

Crop deliberately. Use consistent corner radii or frames. Avoid stretching images out of proportion.

Animation

Use animation to control attention, not to decorate every object. Simple Appear/Fade/Wipe transitions are often enough.

Practice project

Create a 6-slide pitch for a pretend business: title, problem, solution, services, sample results, and call to action. Then redesign it in a second style without changing the content.

Part 4 — Microsoft Access

Access is about relational data. The most important skill is deciding what belongs in separate tables and how those tables connect.

Tables

Store subjects, not reports. Example: Customers, Orders, Services, Payments. Each table should have a primary key.

Relationships

One customer can have many orders. That is a one-to-many relationship: Customers.CustomerID → Orders.CustomerID.

Queries

Queries answer questions. Examples: unpaid orders, customers with more than one order, sales by service, orders due this week.

Forms

Forms make data entry safer and easier than typing directly into tables.

Reports

Reports format database results for printing or sharing.

Practice import

The Access kit includes CSV files and SQL. In Access, create a blank database, import each CSV as a new table, set primary keys, create relationships, then build queries from the exercise list.

Part 5 — Access Practice Exercises

1. Import Customers.csv, Services.csv, Orders.csv, and Payments.csv.

2. Set CustomerID, ServiceID, OrderID, and PaymentID as primary keys.

3. Create one-to-many relationships from Customers to Orders, Services to Orders, and Orders to Payments.

4. Create a query showing all Open orders.

5. Create a query that calculates Balance = QuotedAmount - AmountPaid.

6. Create a parameter query that asks for a customer last name.

7. Create a form for entering new customers.

8. Create an Order Entry form with a customer combo box.

9. Create a report grouped by service.

10. Create a summary query showing revenue by month.

Part 6 — PlayLab Website

Your PlayLab folder contains index.html, styles.css, and app.js. Open index.html in a browser. Use a text editor to change one thing at a time. Refresh the page after saving.

HTML: structure

HTML defines what exists: headings, paragraphs, buttons, forms, sections, links, images, and containers.

CSS: appearance

CSS defines how things look: colors, spacing, fonts, borders, layout, responsive design, shadows, and animations.

JavaScript: behavior

JavaScript makes the page react: clicks, saved notes, games, theme changes, dynamic cards, and drawing.

Safe coding routine

• Make one small change.

• Save the file.

• Refresh the browser.

• If it works, keep going.

• If it breaks, undo the last change or compare with your backup.

• Use the browser Developer Tools console when JavaScript behaves strangely.

Part 7 — 30-Day Practice Plan

Week 1 — Word fundamentals + PlayLab HTML: formatting, styles, tables, headings, edit text and sections.

Week 2 — Excel fundamentals + PlayLab CSS: formulas, tables, conditional formatting, colors, spacing, layouts.

Week 3 — PowerPoint + JavaScript: slide design, layouts, button events, arrays, localStorage.

Week 4 — Access + mini projects: relationships, queries, forms, reports, then combine Office skills into one pretend client project.

Practice Log

Keyboard Shortcuts Worth Learning

When you get stuck

Do not immediately assume you “forgot everything.” First identify the exact step that stopped making sense. Then isolate it. A small question is easier to solve than “Excel is broken” or “my code does not work.” Screenshots and exact error messages are your friends.

Most importantly: practice files are supposed to get messy. That is what makes them useful.

Built to help you practice without being afraid to mess anything up
DateProgramWhat I practicedWhat I learned / need to retry
ShortcutUsually doesPractice idea
Ctrl+C / Ctrl+VCopy / PasteMove content without retyping
Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+YUndo / RedoExperiment fearlessly
Ctrl+SSaveUse constantly
Ctrl+FFindLocate text/data fast
Ctrl+HReplaceBulk text cleanup
Alt+=AutoSum in ExcelQuick totals
F4Repeat / lock refs in Excel formula editingPractice $A$1 references
Ctrl+Shift+LExcel filtersFilter datasets quickly
Ctrl+MNew PowerPoint slideBuild a deck quickly
