title: Once Upon a Thousand Doors
content:
*

ONCE UPON A
THOUSAND DOORS

A Collection of Fairy Tales

Prepared for Templar Hughes-Bryant

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

1

Twenty-five complete retellings and an original fairy tale

novella

Fairy tales have many versions, shaped by centuries of

storytellers. These are fresh, concise retellings of familiar

traditional tales, followed by The Name Beneath the Needle,

an original novella about bargains and true names. The

endings follow recognizable versions, though details vary

across traditions.

Contents

1. Rumpelstiltskin

2. Cinderella

3. Snow White

4. Sleeping Beauty

5. Little Red Riding Hood

6. Hansel and Gretel

7. Rapunzel

8. Beauty and the Beast

9. The Frog Prince

10. The Three Little Pigs

11. Jack and the Beanstalk

12. The Elves and the Shoemaker

13. The Twelve Dancing Princesses

14. The Princess and the Pea

15. The Ugly Duckling

16. The Little Mermaid

17. The Snow Queen

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

2

18. The Emperor's New Clothes

19. The Golden Goose

20. The Bremen Town Musicians

21. The Fisherman and His Wife

22. The Six Swans

23. The Brave Little Tailor

24. The Three Billy Goats Gruff

25. The Three Wishes

26. Bonus novella: The Name Beneath the Needle

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

3

1. Rumpelstiltskin

A miller boasted that his daughter could spin straw into

gold. The king locked her in a room full of straw and

ordered her to prove it. She could not. A small stranger

appeared and offered to do the work for her necklace. The

next night he took her ring. On the third, with nothing left

to give, she promised him her first child.

Years passed. The miller's daughter became queen and

had a baby. The stranger returned to claim the promise.

She pleaded, and he offered one chance: if she could

discover his name in three days, the child would remain

with her.

She sent messengers across the country to collect unusual

names. On the last night, one heard the stranger singing

by a fire in the woods: "Tomorrow I take the royal child;

Rumpelstiltskin is my name." When he came, the queen

spoke the name. His secret power broke, and he departed

in a fury.

The tale begins with a father's foolish boast and a king's

cruel demand. The queen did not choose the impossible

task. Her victory comes when the bargain maker's hidden

advantage is revealed, and she can finally answer him on

equal ground.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

4

2. Cinderella

After her father died, Cinderella lived with a stepmother

and stepsisters who gave her the hardest chores. They

called her by the ashes where she slept. When the royal

celebration was announced, they dressed for the ball and

left her behind.

With help from a magical benefactor, Cinderella received a

beautiful dress, shoes, and a carriage. The magic would

end at midnight. At the ball the prince danced with her,

not knowing her name. She left before the hour struck, but

on a later night fled so quickly that one shoe remained on

the stairs.

The prince searched for the person whose foot fit the shoe.

The stepsisters tried to claim it; Cinderella was finally

allowed to try. It fit. She produced its mate and was

recognized.

Versions disagree about the helper and the fate of the

family. Across them, the story turns on a person whom a

household had made nearly invisible. The shoe is not what

makes Cinderella worthy. It is the small object that forces

others to see the person who had been there all along.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

5

3. Snow White

A queen asked a magic mirror who was fairest. When it

named her stepdaughter Snow White, jealousy hardened

into danger. The girl fled into the forest and found shelter

with seven miners. They warned her not to open the door

to strangers.

The queen came in disguise more than once. At last she

offered a poisoned apple. Snow White bit it and fell into a

deathlike sleep. The miners placed her in a glass coffin

because they could not bear to bury her. A prince later

found her; when the coffin was moved, the piece of apple

came loose, and she woke.

The queen's mirror had answered a narrow question as

though a life could be measured by beauty alone. She

chose to make that answer a threat. Snow White survived

through the care of people who opened their home to her,

though they could not protect her from every trick. When

she woke, the world was wider than the mirror's judgment.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

6

4. Sleeping Beauty

At a princess's birth celebration, an uninvited fairy

foretold that a spindle would wound her. Another softened

the curse: the princess would sleep instead of die, and the

sleep would someday end. The king ordered spindles

removed from his realm.

Years later the princess found an old woman spinning in a

tower. She touched the spindle, and the prophecy took

hold. The castle fell asleep with her. A hedge of thorns

grew around it. Many tried to pass through and failed.

After a hundred years, the hedge opened for a traveler

who reached the castle and found the sleeping princess.

She woke, and the household woke around her.

A kingdom had tried to remove every sharp thing rather

than teach its child about danger. The curse outlasted the

order. Yet the long sleep was not the end of the princess's

story. Morning finally came to a place that had forgotten

what mornings sounded like.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

7

5. Little Red Riding Hood

A child in a red hood carried food to her grandmother

through the woods. Her mother warned her to stay on the

path. A wolf asked where she was going, then took a

shorter route to the grandmother's cottage. He swallowed

the grandmother and lay in her bed to wait.

When the child arrived, she noticed the strange ears, eyes,

and teeth. The wolf swallowed her too. In one familiar

version, a passing woodsman heard him snoring, opened

his belly, and freed them both. They filled the space with

stones, and the wolf could no longer hunt them.

Other versions end much more darkly or let the child

escape by her own wit. The tale survives because a

familiar road can become dangerous when someone uses

trust as a disguise. The questions beside the bed give the

child time to notice what is wrong. In the gentler ending,

she and her grandmother get another day together.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

8

6. Hansel and Gretel

During a famine, two children were abandoned in the

forest. Hansel had scattered pebbles on the first journey

and led Gretel home. The second time he had only bread

crumbs, and birds ate them. Lost, the children found a

house made of sweets. Its owner welcomed them in, then

trapped Hansel and set Gretel to work.

The witch planned to eat Hansel. Gretel pretended not to

understand how to inspect the oven. When the witch bent

forward to show her, Gretel pushed her inside and closed

the door. She freed her brother. They found the witch's

treasure and made their way home, where the parent who

had abandoned them was gone.

The sweet walls had promised food to hungry children and

concealed a greater hunger. Hansel's first plan saved them

once; Gretel's quick judgment saved them at the end. They

returned with enough to live, but their courage had been

required because the adults charged with protecting them

had failed.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

9

7. Rapunzel

A couple took greens from a sorceress's garden, and the

sorceress demanded their unborn child in payment. She

named the girl Rapunzel and raised her in a tower with no

stairs. When she came to visit, she called for Rapunzel to

lower her long hair.

A prince heard Rapunzel singing and learned the call.

They met in secret and planned an escape. The sorceress

discovered them, cut Rapunzel's hair, and sent her away.

She deceived the prince at the tower; he fell and lost his

sight.

After wandering for years, he heard Rapunzel's voice

again. They found one another, and her tears restored his

sight in a familiar version. They left the tower's power

behind.

The girl had been treated as payment for someone else's

act. The tower kept her safe from ordinary roads but also

kept her from choosing one. Her song carried beyond its

walls before she ever did. In the end, she and the prince

recognized each other by a voice no one could lock away.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

10

8. Beauty and the Beast

A merchant sought shelter in an enchanted castle and

picked a rose for his daughter Beauty. The Beast, master

of the castle, demanded a life for the flower. Beauty chose

to go in her father's place. The Beast treated her kindly

and asked her to marry him each evening; she refused,

though friendship grew between them.

Beauty was allowed to visit her family, but she stayed

longer than promised. In a dream she saw the Beast dying

alone. She returned and found him in the garden. She said

she loved him and would stay. The enchantment broke,

revealing a prince.

The tale can be read as a lesson about looking beyond

appearances, but Beauty's freedom to leave and return

matters too. Her answer had value because it was hers to

give. The rose began as a thoughtless gift; the final choice

came from knowing the person who had lived in the castle

with her.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

11

9. The Frog Prince

A princess dropped her golden ball into a deep well. A frog

offered to retrieve it if she would welcome him as a

companion. She agreed, then ran away as soon as the ball

was in her hands. The frog came to the palace and

demanded that she keep her word.

Her father insisted on the promise. Reluctantly she let the

frog eat beside her and enter her room. In versions of the

tale, the enchantment breaks after a kiss, an angry act, or

simply the fulfillment of the agreement. The frog becomes

a prince.

The transformation often overshadows the odd friendship

that precedes it. The princess had wanted her ball back

without taking seriously the creature who helped her. The

frog had asked for a place at the table, not for gold. The

tale keeps changing because tellers disagree about

whether its heart is a kept promise, a change of feeling, or

the surprise that someone despised may have a hidden

life.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

12

10. The Three Little Pigs

Three pigs built homes of straw, sticks, and brick. A wolf

came to the straw house and blew it down. The first pig

escaped to the second, but the stick house fell as well.

Together they ran to the brick house, where the third pig

had taken more time and care.

The wolf huffed, puffed, and could not bring it down. He

tried the chimney instead. The pigs prepared a pot of hot

water beneath it, and the wolf fled when he saw he had

been outwitted.

The story's rhythm invites listeners to predict what comes

next. Its lesson about preparation is familiar, but there is

another detail worth keeping: the pigs who built quickly

were not left outside when danger came. The strongest

house sheltered all three. A wall is useful because of whom

it protects.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

13

11. Jack and the Beanstalk

Jack traded the family cow for magic beans, angering his

mother. Overnight a beanstalk rose into the clouds. Jack

climbed it and found a giant's house. The giant's wife hid

him. He took a bag of gold and escaped. On later visits he

carried away a hen that laid golden eggs and a singing

harp.

The giant chased him down the beanstalk. Jack cut it, and

the giant fell. Jack and his mother had enough to live on

thereafter.

Some tellers call Jack brave; others notice that he stole

from a house where he had entered uninvited. Versions

sometimes give the giant a history of stealing from Jack's

family, changing the moral shape of the adventure. What

remains is the irresistible image of an impossible ladder

growing from a poor household's last hope. Jack climbed

without knowing what he would find above the clouds.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

14

12. The Elves and the Shoemaker

A poor shoemaker had leather enough for one pair of

shoes. He cut the pieces and went to bed. In the morning a

beautifully made pair stood on his bench. He sold it,

bought more leather, and found another set of shoes

finished overnight. The work continued until his family

was secure.

One night he and his wife watched from hiding. Two small

elves came in and stitched with extraordinary speed. The

couple saw that the elves wore almost nothing in winter.

They made them tiny clothes and shoes. The elves dressed

with delight, danced away, and never returned.

The shoemaker had received help without demanding to

know its source. Once he did know, he answered with a

gift that suited the helpers rather than a bargain that

would keep them working. The elves left, and the

shoemaker carried on with his own hands. Gratitude did

not mean trying to own their labor.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

15

13. The Twelve Dancing Princesses

Every morning twelve princesses' shoes were worn

through, though their door had been locked all night. Their

father offered a reward to anyone who could solve the

mystery. Many failed. A soldier received a cloak of

invisibility from an old woman and followed the sisters

after they pretended to sleep.

They passed through a hidden door to a glittering

underground kingdom and danced until dawn. The soldier

returned with proof: branches from the strange trees and

a cup from the hall. He revealed their secret to the king.

The familiar ending rewards him, often with marriage to

the eldest princess. Yet the secret dance remains the most

vivid part of the story. The sisters had found a world

beyond a locked bedroom and shared its entrance with one

another. The worn shoes told the truth before anyone

knew how to read it: their nights belonged to a life the

palace could not see.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

16

14. The Princess and the Pea

A prince wanted to marry a real princess, though he could

not decide what that meant. On a stormy night a young

woman arrived at the palace, wet and asking for shelter.

She said she was a princess. The queen placed a pea

beneath a high stack of mattresses and bedding.

In the morning the guest said she had slept badly because

something hard had pressed against her. The queen took

this sensitivity as proof of royal birth. The prince married

her, and the pea was kept as a curiosity.

The tale is so small that it feels like a joke played with

great seriousness. The palace had searched for certainty

in titles and appearances. Its test was a vegetable beneath

a mountain of blankets. Perhaps the princess was

unusually sensitive; perhaps the queen believed what she

wished to believe. Either way, the pea became more

famous than the guest's name.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

17

15. The Ugly Duckling

A large gray chick hatched among ducklings who mocked

his looks. He left the farm and endured a hard winter,

never finding a place where he felt welcome. When spring

came, he saw swans on a lake and approached them,

expecting to be rejected again. In the water he saw his

reflection: he had grown into a swan.

The others welcomed him. Children on the shore admired

the beautiful newcomer. He remembered the cold, the

jeers, and the long lonely days. Their kindness did not

erase those seasons, but he no longer had to live inside the

judgment of creatures who had misunderstood him.

The story is sometimes told as though a person must

become beautiful to deserve care. Its deeper sadness lies

in how long the young swan was mistreated while he was

already himself. His nature did not begin when the

reflection changed. He had needed warmth all along.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

18

16. The Little Mermaid

A mermaid longed to know the human world and loved a

prince she had saved from a wreck. She went to a sea

witch, who gave her legs in exchange for her voice.

Walking would hurt, and if the prince married someone

else, she would face death at dawn.

On land the prince cared for her but did not know she had

rescued him. He married another. The mermaid's sisters

offered her a way to return to the sea if she harmed him.

She refused. At sunrise she cast herself into the waves and

became a spirit of the air in the traditional literary tale.

Later versions soften or change the ending. The older

story is about desire, sacrifice, and a voice surrendered for

a chance to be seen. The mermaid's final choice is not

rewarded with the prince. It is hers nonetheless. She

refuses to make another person pay for the bargain she

made.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

19

17. The Snow Queen

A shard from a wicked mirror entered young Kay's eye and

heart, making beauty look ugly and kindness seem foolish.

The Snow Queen carried him away to her frozen palace.

His friend Gerda set out to find him. She crossed gardens,

rivers, and strange kingdoms, helped by people and

creatures who listened to her story.

At last Gerda reached Kay. He sat arranging pieces of ice,

unable to remember home. Her tears warmed him and

washed the mirror's splinter away. He recognized her.

Together they returned, older than when they had parted,

to a place where roses still grew.

Gerda had no sword and no grand title. Her journey was

held together by affection and persistence. The Snow

Queen's palace was beautiful and empty of warmth. The

puzzle of ice could not give Kay what a familiar voice and a

friend's tears restored.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

20

18. The Emperor's New Clothes

Two swindlers told an emperor they could weave cloth

invisible to anyone foolish or unfit for office. They worked

at empty looms and collected costly thread. The emperor

and his officials saw nothing, but each praised the fabric

rather than risk admitting it.

The emperor paraded through the city wearing the

supposed garments. The crowd admired what it could not

see. A child finally cried that the emperor had no clothes.

Others repeated it, and the truth spread along the street.

The emperor continued walking, aware that the child was

right.

The swindlers' trick depended less on magic than on a fear

of looking foolish. Everyone could have spoken sooner. The

child's observation did not require special wisdom, only

freedom from the pressure that kept the adults silent.

Once one voice named the obvious, the whole city could

see it together.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

21

19. The Golden Goose

A younger son, dismissed as simple by his family, shared

his small meal with an old stranger. In return he found a

goose with golden feathers. People tried to pluck a feather

for themselves and became stuck to the bird. Anyone who

tried to pull them free stuck to the person ahead, until a

ridiculous procession followed the young man down the

road.

A princess who had never laughed saw the line and burst

into laughter. Her father had promised her hand to

whoever could make her laugh, though he tried to set

further tasks before keeping his word. With the stranger's

help, the young man completed them and married the

princess.

The tale enjoys the spectacle of greedy hands caught in

the act. The young man did not set out to humiliate

anyone. He began by sharing a meal when he had little to

spare. The golden goose came after that kindness; the

train of grasping strangers came after people forgot it.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

22

20. The Bremen Town Musicians

A donkey too old for his farmer's work ran away to become

a musician in Bremen. On the road he met a dog, a cat,

and a rooster, each abandoned or threatened because age

had made them less useful to an owner. They traveled

together.

At night they found a house occupied by robbers. The

animals stacked themselves in the window and made a

tremendous noise. The robbers fled, believing some

terrible creature had arrived. The four companions ate

supper and settled in. When a robber returned, their teeth,

claws, hooves, and crowing frightened him away for good.

They never reached Bremen. They had set out looking for

a place to belong and found one before the city gates.

Their music may not have been beautiful, but together

they made a sound no one could ignore.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

23

21. The Fisherman and His Wife

A fisherman caught a talking fish who said he was an

enchanted prince. He let it go. His wife asked him to

return and request a better home. The fish granted it.

Soon she wanted a grander house, then a palace, then

greater and greater power. Each time the fisherman went

to the shore, the sea grew darker.

At last she demanded a power beyond any human station.

The fish gave no speech about greed. When the fisherman

returned, he found their old small home, as it had been

before the wishes.

The fisherman was uneasy from the start but carried each

request anyway. His wife's wanting grew, and his

reluctance did not stop him from asking. The changing sea

measured the trouble more honestly than either of them

did. At the end, they had shelter, food, and one another,

though it was for them to decide whether they could live

with that.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

24

22. The Six Swans

A king's six sons were turned into swans by a spell. Their

sister learned that she could free them by sewing six shirts

of starflowers while remaining silent for six years. She

worked in the woods, gathering flowers and stitching

without a word.

A neighboring king found and married her. His mother

mistrusted the silent young queen and accused her of

terrible deeds. She could not defend herself without

breaking the spell. As she was led to her execution, the six

years ended. The swans flew overhead. She threw the

finished shirts onto them, and her brothers became human

again. One shirt lacked a sleeve, leaving its brother with a

swan's wing.

At last she spoke and told her story. The unfinished sleeve

remains an important detail. Her courage saved her

brothers, but the work had been done under conditions no

one could meet perfectly. The brother with the wing lived,

marked by what they had survived together.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

25

23. The Brave Little Tailor

A tailor killed seven flies with one blow and made a belt

reading "Seven at One Blow." Others assumed he had

defeated seven men. He did not correct them. Sent against

giants and dangerous beasts, he used quick thinking to

make his opponents defeat themselves.

A king promised rewards for these feats, then tried to

escape his promise when the tailor succeeded. The tailor

uncovered the plans against him and kept both his life and

his prize.

The belt was true in the narrowest possible sense. Its

readers supplied the grander story. The tailor survived

because he noticed what people expected and used it. His

courage was real, even if the original seven had wings and

fit on a piece of bread. The tale laughs at powerful people

who mistake a reputation for knowledge.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

26

24. The Three Billy Goats Gruff

Three goats wanted to cross a bridge to a hillside where

the grass was rich. A troll lived beneath the bridge and

threatened to eat anyone who passed. The smallest goat

went first. When the troll leaped up, the little goat said a

larger brother was coming and would make a better meal.

The troll let him pass.

The middle goat crossed next and made the same promise

about the largest. At last the great goat stepped onto the

boards. The troll sprang out, expecting an easy feast. This

time the goat met him with strong horns and drove him

from the bridge. All three reached the green hillside.

The little goats escaped by thinking quickly, and the eldest

could face the danger they had delayed. Their plan worked

because they trusted one another to follow. The bridge did

not change; the troll did not become kind. Together the

goats made a way across a place none of them could safely

cross in the same way alone.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

27

25. The Three Wishes

A couple were granted three wishes and promised to use

them wisely. They spent an evening arguing over palaces,

riches, and long lives. Hungry and tired, one wished for a

sausage. It appeared on the table. The other, angry that a

wish had been wasted, wished the sausage onto the first

one's nose.

After struggling to pull it free, they used the final wish to

remove it. Their home was as it had been. They ate a plain

supper and laughed, eventually, at the fortune that had

come and gone before they had made a plan.

The story is comic because the magic obeys exactly what is

said, not what is meant. The couple had imagined wishes

as a way to avoid ordinary limits. In the end they still had

to share a meal, forgive a foolish moment, and decide what

mattered without anyone granting it for them.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

28

Bonus Original Novella

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

29

THE NAME BENEATH THE
NEEDLE

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

30

An original fairy tale novella

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

31

Prologue: The Thirteenth Stitch

In the village of Bellwether, every child learned to count to

twelve before learning to count to thirteen. Twelve

stitches made a buttonhole strong. Twelve bells warned of

a storm. Twelve chairs stood at the mayor's table. The

thirteenth stitch, people said, gave a garment a place to

hide a secret.

Mara Vell did not believe cloth could keep secrets. People

kept them. Cloth only showed where their hands had

trembled.

Her father had been a tailor so skilled he could cut a coat

that made a shy man stand straight. After his death, Mara

inherited three needles, a narrow shop, and a debt owed to

Lord Varrow, who owned the mill and half the houses in

Bellwether. He gave her until the Harvest Fair to pay. On

the first day of autumn, he arrived with a wagon of gray

cloth.

"Make a coat from this," he said. "A coat that will cause

everyone who sees me to love me."

"I cannot sew love into cloth."

"Then sew me something close enough," he replied. "If you

fail, your shop becomes mine."

He left the cloth and a smile that lasted exactly as long as

it took him to reach the street.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

32

Mara held the fabric to the light. Hidden in its weave was

a thirteenth thread, finer than spider silk and blacker than

an unlit window. When she pulled it, a voice beneath her

worktable said, "Careful. That thread is attached to

someone."

A small man unfolded himself from the shadow. His coat

had buttons made from mismatched coins, and his eyes

were the pale gold of old candle wax.

"Who are you?" Mara asked.

"A person with an offer."

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

33

Chapter One: A Bargain with Edges

The stranger called himself Mister Nettle, though he said

it with the air of a person borrowing an umbrella. He

offered to make the coat overnight. By morning Lord

Varrow would be admired wherever he went. The price

was one memory Mara would not miss.

"How can I know I won't miss it?" she asked.

"You won't remember having it."

It was a neat answer that explained nothing. Mara refused.

Nettle tipped his hat and disappeared beneath the table,

leaving no footprints in the dust. She worked through the

night herself. By dawn she had a plain, fine coat and

pricked fingers. She delivered it to Varrow's manor.

He put it on before a mirror. "Do I look beloved?"

"You look well dressed," Mara said.

He marched into the market to test it. People

complimented the cut, then stepped around him to

continue their errands. An apple seller asked him to pay

what he owed from last week. A child hid behind her

mother. Varrow returned furious.

"Three nights," he said. "Make it work, or the shop is

mine."

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

34

That evening Mara visited the oldest person in Bellwether,

Grandmother Pell, who repaired umbrellas and claimed to

have outlived three kings and two fashions for pointy

shoes. Pell examined the black thread under a magnifying

lens.

"This is a binding," she said. "Someone's promise has been

spun into the cloth. Varrow knows it."

"Can I remove it?"

"Ask what was promised and to whom. Then decide

whether you want to honor it."

Pell would say no more. Mara returned home to find Nettle

sitting in the window with a pear he had taken from her

bowl. He offered the same bargain, now for a memory of

her choosing.

"If you can make him loved," she said, "why did you not do

it before he came to me?"

Nettle bit into the pear. "He asked for love without doing

anything lovable. Those requests are difficult."

"Then your coat would be a trick."

"Most coats are," he said. "They persuade the eye before

the wearer speaks."

Mara did not send him away. She asked him to teach her

how the black thread worked. Nettle's face became wary.

A bargain that could be understood was less useful to him.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

35

Chapter Two: The Mill at Midnight

At midnight Nettle led Mara to the mill. Its wheel turned

though the stream had run nearly dry. Inside, looms

clattered without hands. The black thread ran through

every bolt of gray cloth and vanished through a locked

door beneath the floor.

"The cloth listens," Nettle said. "Varrow can ask it to carry

a wish, but only if someone else bears the cost."

Mara knelt beside the looms. Tiny words were woven into

the selvedge: warmth from Bera; rest from Tomas;

courage from Elin. The mill had been taking small

comforts from its workers for years. Bera, who had once

laughed loudly in the market, now shivered in summer.

Tomas slept at his loom because he could never feel

rested. Elin would not cross the little bridge to visit her

sister.

"You helped him," Mara said.

"I made the first loom," Nettle replied. "He learned to feed

it."

The locked door shook. From below came the sound of

someone humming a tune Mara recognized: her father's

work song. He had died before the mill was built. She

followed the sound until Nettle grabbed her sleeve.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

36

"It borrows voices," he said. "It knows which one would

make you open the door."

Mara pulled free, but she did not open it. She placed her

ear against the boards. The humming stopped. A different

voice, thin and frightened, whispered, "Tell them we are

here."

They returned to the shop with a scrap of cloth. Nettle

showed her how to unpick a binding without snapping it.

Each black thread had to be traced back to the hand that

had given something away. Cut it too soon and the stolen

gift might never find its owner.

"Why teach me?" Mara asked.

Nettle wound a thread around his finger. "I am tired of

mending the lies that come out of that room."

It was the first thing he had said that sounded like an

answer.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

37

Chapter Three: The Girl Who Lost
Her Laugh

Mara began with Bera. The mill worker could remember

jokes but could no longer laugh at them. She feared that

the loss had made her unkind, although she still brought

soup to every sick neighbor. Mara showed her the woven

words.

"Varrow asked me to sign a paper when I started," Bera

said. "It said the mill might keep a portion of my joy during

busy seasons. I thought that was a figure of speech."

Mara opened the seam of a gray shawl Bera had worn for

years. The black thread lay there, looped thirteen times.

She loosened each loop while Bera named a moment she

had enjoyed: the smell of bread, a niece learning to

whistle, a rainy afternoon with nowhere to go. On the last

loop, Bera laughed at the absurd sound of her own rusty

whistle. The shawl turned a shade lighter.

Word traveled. Tomas came with his cap. Elin came with a

ribbon from the mill. Mara worked slowly. She could not

restore a stolen thing by pretending she knew what it had

meant to its owner. Each person had to describe it in their

own words.

At dusk Varrow arrived. The workers had begun

questioning their contracts. He blamed Mara. He offered

to forgive the debt if she finished the coat and kept silent

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

38

about the mill.

"You cannot make them love you," she said.

"I can make them grateful," he replied. "I provide the work

that feeds them."

"You have taken part of the people who do it."

He seized the unfinished coat and carried it away. Mara

ran after him, but the market clock struck twelve. Nettle

appeared between them and held up a finger.

"You have a night," he told Varrow. "Wear it before it is

finished and the wish may turn inside out."

Varrow stopped. He threw the coat back at Mara.

"Tomorrow, then."

When he had gone, Nettle looked ill. "I lied," he admitted.

"There is no such rule. But I can only lie to him once. He

has my true name."

Mara understood then why he used Mister Nettle. Names

in Bellwether were not merely ways to call someone; some

could be used like keys.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

39

Chapter Four: The Locked Room

Grandmother Pell arrived at Mara's shop after dark,

carrying a ring of keys and a loaf of bread. "I should have

told you sooner," she said. "I helped Varrow build the room

under the mill. I thought it would store old promises

safely. I did not ask who decided what a promise was

worth."

The three of them went to the mill while the workers

gathered outside. Pell opened the floor door. Beneath it

was a chamber lined with glass bottles. Each held a glow

or shadow: Bera's laughter had been one, Tomas's rest

another. Hundreds remained. At the center stood a loom

larger than the others, with a card pinned to it: THE

OWNER MAY CLAIM WHAT IS GIVEN.

"The paper they signed," Mara said.

"The words were hidden in plain sight," Pell replied. "That

does not make them fair."

In a bottle near the back, Mara found the work song she

had heard. It held a fragment of her father's voice, taken

years earlier when he had tailored Varrow's wedding

clothes. The sound ached in her chest. She reached for it,

then stopped. It was not all that remained of him. His

patient stitches, his silly drawings in the pattern books,

and her own memories lived elsewhere.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

40

Nettle touched an empty bottle. "Mine is not here," he

said. "Varrow keeps my name in his signet ring. He makes

me answer whenever he turns it."

He had designed the loom long ago to hold spoken

promises for people who feared they would forget. Varrow

had turned it into a machine for taking more than anyone

intended to give. Nettle had stayed partly from guilt,

partly because a ring on another man's hand could

summon him from any road.

Above them, heavy steps crossed the mill floor. Varrow

had come early. Pell closed the room's outer door, but the

lock would not hold him long.

Mara examined the great loom. Its threads ran through

every bottle. If she cut them all, the contents could scatter.

If she left them, Varrow would keep drawing from the

workers. She needed a way for each stolen thing to find its

own person.

"A thirteenth stitch," Pell said. "A place to hide a secret."

Mara shook her head. "A place to carry it," she answered.

She began a new seam around the coat's lining, leaving

one open space after every twelve stitches.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

41

Chapter Five: The Coat of Many
Voices

By dawn Mara had sewn a lining of hundreds of small

pockets. She placed a thread from each bottle into its own

pocket, and beside it she stitched the name of the person

from whom it had been taken. She did not know every

name. For those she left a space and asked Pell to call the

workers down one by one.

The chamber became crowded. People spoke over each

other, eager and angry. Mara asked them to slow down. A

lost thing could not be returned simply because someone

shouted loudest. They traced the threads. Bera recognized

a joke she had told her brother. Tomas recognized a

morning when he had awakened ready to work. Elin

recognized the small courage that had once carried her

across the bridge.

As each person spoke, a bottle opened, and the light inside

followed its thread home. Some gifts returned at once;

others settled slowly, like feeling in a hand after cold. No

one emerged exactly as they had been. They had lived

through the loss, too, and that experience belonged to

them.

Varrow broke through the outer door carrying his signet

ring. He saw the workers around his bottles and ordered

Nettle to stop Mara. Nettle staggered forward against his

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

42

own will.

"Do not say your name," he whispered to her. "He will put

it in the ring as well."

Varrow demanded the coat. Mara handed it to him. He put

it on, sure that its hidden threads would grant his wish. In

the market above, the fair bells began to ring. The

garment drew every eye. For one long breath, the crowd

regarded him in silence.

Then the voices stitched into its lining spoke. Not in

praise, and not as a spell of hatred. Each told a small true

thing: a promise Varrow had twisted, a wage he had

withheld, a kindness someone else had done despite him.

The voices did not force the crowd to feel anything. They

gave people facts that had been kept apart.

Varrow tore at the lining. The thirteenth spaces released

the remaining threads into the air. They flew toward their

owners, leaving the coat plain and gray. He fled from the

mill with no admirers following.

But Nettle fell to his knees. Varrow still held the ring. As

long as the true name stayed inside it, one command could

bring him back.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

43

Chapter Six: The Name Game

Mara and Pell followed Varrow through the fair. He

reached the old clock tower and threatened to command

Nettle to rebuild the loom. The ring flashed whenever he

spoke the borrowed name, but Mara could not hear the

word. It slipped from her mind the instant it was said.

"How do we take it from him?" she asked.

"A true name must be given back by its holder," Pell

replied. "Or the holder must willingly give up the power it

grants."

Varrow laughed from the tower steps. Willingly was the

last thing he intended.

Mara thought of a dozen fairy stories in which a clever

guess broke a bargain. She could try names all day and

learn nothing. She needed to understand why Varrow

clung to this one.

"What did you want before you wanted everyone to love

you?" she called.

He looked startled. "What kind of question is that?"

"A simple one."

He had grown up poor, he said, and people had laughed at

the patch on his only coat. He had sworn never to be at

anyone's mercy again. Owning the mill, the houses, and

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

44

finally Nettle's name had felt like a way to keep the world

from laughing.

Mara did not excuse what he had done. Fear could explain

a cruelty without paying its victims back. But she could

see a path through his pride.

"The ring cannot make you safe," she said. "Every person

you bind gives you another reason to fear them."

For a moment his hand loosened. Then the mayor arrived

with two guards. He ordered Varrow to surrender the ring.

Varrow's fear hardened. He shouted Nettle's name and

commanded him to bring the great loom to the square.

Nettle rose unwillingly. Mara caught his arm. "Tell me one

thing about yourself that he cannot command," she said.

Nettle's face worked with effort. "I once made a blue kite

for a girl who was afraid of the wind."

"What was her name?"

He smiled through pain. "I do not remember. She grew up.

That was enough."

He took one step toward the mill, then another. The

command held his feet but not his mind. Mara ran to the

bell tower's mechanism, where twelve ropes hung for

twelve bells. She tied the loose red thread from her coat to

a thirteenth place between them.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

45

When she pulled, no bell rang. Instead the fair heard

Nettle's story in his own voice.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

46

Chapter Seven: The Bell Without a
Bell

Nettle spoke of the loom as it had been: a place for

promises people wished to keep, tended by consent. He

spoke of his mistake in trusting Varrow with the keys. He

spoke of the years he had been afraid to resist because

one stolen word could drag him back.

The sound traveled through the thirteenth thread in the

coat and through every loosened binding in Bellwether.

The mill workers heard it. So did those who had never

signed a contract but had enjoyed cheap cloth without

asking its cost.

Varrow commanded silence. Nettle's mouth closed, but the

people continued the account. Pell admitted her part. Bera

named her loss. Others named theirs. The story no longer

depended on one voice.

The mayor reached for the ring. Mara stopped him. If he

took it without changing the terms, the power would

simply move to a new hand.

"Offer it back," she told Varrow. "No bargain. No prize."

Varrow stared at the ring. He had wanted a crowd to love

him. Now the crowd watched him without affection, but

also without the laughter he had feared since childhood.

They waited for his choice.

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

47

He removed the ring. For a moment he seemed likely to

throw it into the river, where anyone might find it. Instead

he held it out to Nettle.

"I give up the claim," he said.

Nettle took the ring. The true name did not pass aloud. It

returned to him like a breath drawn after too long under

water. He crushed the signet against a stone. The metal

split, and no spell answered.

The mayor's guards took Varrow to answer for the

withheld wages and stolen comforts. The villagers did not

decide his future in a single angry hour. They made a list

of what had been taken, listened to those who bore the

cost, and set about making repairs. Some damage could be

paid for. Some could only be acknowledged and never

repeated.

Nettle could have left as soon as the ring broke. He stayed

long enough to help dismantle the great loom. The original

small loom, which held only promises freely entrusted to

it, he carried to Mara's shop and placed by the window.

"Will you use it?" he asked.

"Only if I can explain every thread to the person who owns

it," she said.

"A difficult rule."

"A good one."

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

48

Chapter Eight: A Coat for Winter

Winter came early to Bellwether. Mara's shop filled with

ordinary work: torn sleeves, lost buttons, coats for

children who had grown since spring. People no longer

asked her to sew feelings into garments. They asked for

pockets deep enough to hold warm stones and seams

strong enough to survive snow.

Varrow's mill reopened under the workers' care. Its

contracts were read aloud and written plainly. Anyone

could leave without surrendering a piece of themselves.

The cloth it made was slower and more expensive, but

Bera laughed as she worked, and Tomas went home at

dusk to sleep.

One evening Nettle returned wearing a coat with all its

buttons matching, which Mara found suspicious. He

brought a small parcel. Inside lay a needle made of dark

wood. It had belonged, he said, to the first keeper of

honest promises.

"I have my name back," he told her, "but I have not

decided whether to share it."

"You don't owe it to me."

"I know. That is why I might."

He sat by the window and watched Mara sew. At the

thirteenth stitch of a child's coat, she paused. There was

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

49

room for a secret if she wanted one. Instead she made a

plain strong seam and asked the child's mother to test it

with a gentle pull.

Later that night, Mara took her father's old pattern book

from the shelf. Between sketches of collars and cuffs she

found a note in his handwriting: A good coat lets a person

go where they choose. She had read it before. This time

she understood it differently.

The little loom by the window held one promise. Mara had

placed it there herself: that she would tell the truth about

what her work could do, and what it could not. It needed

no bottle or black thread. It required her to keep choosing

it.

Outside, thirteen bells sounded in the wind. The villagers

had added one to mark the hour at which the mill had

opened its doors. Children no longer skipped from twelve

to fourteen when they counted. They shouted thirteen with

special pleasure, as children do when adults have been

foolish about a number.

Nettle, still at the window, said his true name softly. Mara

heard it. She did not write it down or repeat it to anyone

else. A gift freely offered could be held without being used.

In the years that followed, people told the story in

different ways. Some made Mara a princess, though she

had never owned a crown. Some gave Nettle horns,

though his hat had covered only hair. Mara corrected what

mattered: the workers had freed themselves together; the

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

50

coat had told truths, not manufactured love; and nobody's

name had been won by a clever guess.

As for the rest, she let the tellers have their embroidery.

Every fairy tale needs a little. But when a child asked what

the magic had really been, Mara held up a needle and said,

"A stitch can join two things. The choice of what to join is

ours."

ONCE UPON A THOUSAND DOORS

51

Author's Note

This is an original fairy tale. It draws on the broader

tradition of bargains, true names, impossible tasks, and

clever makers, but its characters, plot, and setting are

newly written.
