04_Review_Notes/

05_Final_Delivery/

Naming example: ClientName_Flyer_v01.pdf for a draft and ClientName_Flyer_FINAL.pdf for approved delivery. Avoid naming a draft FINAL before approval.

Lesson 1 Website Design

Responsive websites and digital experiences

What this service teaches

Information architecture. Organize pages around what visitors need to find and do. A visitor should be able to reach services, proof of work, and contact from clear navigation.

Responsive layout. Use flexible widths, grid, and breakpoints so content adapts to a phone without tiny text or sideways scrolling.

Interaction and data. A visual button is not a completed feature. A working form requires validation, server handling, confirmation, and safe storage or delivery.

Accessibility. Use meaningful headings, labels, keyboard operation, alt text, and readable contrast so more people can use the site.

Worked example

Worked example: For a cafe, a visitor wants hours, menu, location, and contact. Put hours and a Menu link near the top; add a clear address and accessible contact path. On a phone, stack the menu cards. Test every link and the real contact delivery before saying the form works.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A beautiful contact form displays “Sent” but no email or record is created. Is the job complete? Explain the missing components.

Model answer: No. The interface is a visual prototype. It needs reliable server-side delivery or storage, error handling, and an end-to-end test.

Client situation

A small business wants a five-page site that visitors can use on a phone.

Ask before you begin

• What pages, actions, and content are required?

• Who owns the domain and hosting account?

• Is there an existing logo, brand guide, privacy notice, and approved copy?

• Does the site need accounts, payments, booking, or a database? These change scope substantially.

Do the job step by step

1. Make a page list and a simple navigation map: Home, About, Services, Portfolio, Contact.

2. Collect approved text, photos, logo files, contact links, and any required policy text. Record missing items.

3. Sketch mobile and desktop layouts with headings, calls to action, and clear reading order.

4. Build semantic HTML and responsive CSS. Add JavaScript only for behavior the site needs.

5. Check every link, form, button, image, and path. Do not label a form as working until messages actually arrive.

6. Test narrow and wide screens, keyboard navigation, readable contrast, image alt text, and loading speed.

7. Review with the client on a private preview. Record requested changes and obtain approval.

8. Make a backup, publish to the agreed hosting account, then retest the live URL and document the handoff.

Check your work

• Five page links work in both directions.

• No placeholder wording or broken images remain.

• Mobile view has no horizontal overflow.

• Forms and dynamic features are tested end to end, or clearly labeled as demos.

• Client receives ownership and maintenance information for accounts and files.

Practice assignment

Build a fictional three-page site for Muffins N Mocha: Home, Menu, Contact. Use a working navigation menu, a responsive layout, and a practice-only contact form that clearly says it does not send messages.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 2 Branding & Creative

Flyers, banners, invitations, advertisements, and social graphics

What this service teaches

Audience and purpose. A flyer, church program, invitation, and banner serve different reading situations. Identify what someone should notice and do first.

Visual hierarchy. Use size, contrast, and spacing to rank information. A headline, date, location, and action should not compete equally.

Typography and image quality. Choose legible fonts and use images with enough resolution for the actual output. Stretching a small image does not create detail.

Print production. Trim removes edges. Bleed extends artwork beyond trim; safe margins keep important text inside. Confirm printer specifications before export.

Worked example

Worked example: A church program cover needs event title, date, venue, and a dignified image. Inside pages carry the order of service and names. First arrange the approved text in reading order, then style it. Print a test page at actual size to catch tiny names and weak contrast.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: The event date is correct on the flyer but wrong on the matching social graphic. What should you do?

Model answer: Correct the social graphic, compare both files against the approved brief, and send a fresh proof for confirmation.

Client situation

A client requests a church program and a matching flyer for an event.

Ask before you begin

• What exact words, date, time, location, names, and spelling must appear?

• What is the intended print or digital size?

• Are photos, logos, and colors approved and high enough quality?

• What is the order of importance: headline, event details, call to action?

Do the job step by step

1. Ask for the content in writing and mark anything missing; verify names and dates with the client.

2. Create a visual hierarchy so a reader notices the main message first.

3. Choose two readable typefaces or a restrained type system and a consistent palette.

4. Set the correct page size and safe margins before designing. Allow space for printer trimming when requested.

5. Place content and images. Check licensing or the client’s permission to use supplied imagery.

6. Proofread each line against the approved source, including phone, address, time zone, and website.

7. Export a review PDF or image, gather consolidated feedback, revise, and request final approval.

8. Export the agreed print and digital formats; keep editable source files organized.

Check your work

• All mandatory information is present and legible at intended size.

• No text sits too close to the trim edge.

• Photos are sharp and not stretched.

• Spelling and dates match the approved brief.

• Final files have descriptive names and the agreed dimensions.

Practice assignment

Design a fictional two-page church program and a matching event flyer. Make a content checklist before opening the design tool. Proofread from bottom to top after the first draft.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 3 Business Tools

Custom forms, workflows, customer-facing tools, and automation concepts

What this service teaches

Process mapping. Write down who begins a request, who reviews it, what decisions occur, and when work ends. The tool should follow that process.

Form design. Ask only for data needed to complete the task. Labels, required fields, and errors should be clear.

State design. Statuses such as New, Waiting, and Complete must have defined meanings and allowed transitions.

Testing and permissions. Try unusual input and interrupted work. Confirm each person sees only the records they are allowed to see.

Worked example

Worked example: A request tracker begins at New. An owner checks details and moves it to Reviewing. If a required file is absent, it moves to Waiting with a reason. Once supplied, it returns to Reviewing. The client receives a clear status rather than an unexplained color.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A request can move from New directly to Complete without anyone reviewing it. What is wrong?

Model answer: The process lacks an approval or work step. Define a valid transition and a responsible person before implementing the status change.

Client situation

A small organization wants a request form and a simple status tracker.

Ask before you begin

• What information is truly necessary?

• Who may see or edit each record?

• Which steps happen after submission, and who owns each step?

• What must happen when a form fails or a duplicate is submitted?

Do the job step by step

1. Map the current process as intake, review, decision, work, and closeout.

2. List fields with their purpose; remove unnecessary sensitive data.

3. Sketch the form and status states before building. Define required fields and helpful error text.

4. Build a prototype with fictional records. Keep secrets and privileged actions on a server, never in public HTML.

5. Test empty input, invalid input, long input, duplicate submission, and interrupted connection.

6. Check keyboard use, labels, readable feedback, and privacy of each view.

7. Demonstrate the process to the client and document who maintains it.

8. Deliver the agreed tool plus a one-page usage guide and a backup plan.

Check your work

• Every field has a clear label and purpose.

• Errors tell the user what to fix without erasing their work.

• Unauthorized users cannot see or change private records.

• The workflow has an owner for each step.

• The client can use and maintain the tool after handoff.

Practice assignment

Build a practice request tracker using five fictional entries and statuses New, Reviewing, Waiting, In Progress, and Complete. Write the rules for moving between statuses.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 4 Career & Office

Resumes, cover letters, bios, and Microsoft Office work

What this service teaches

Evidence-based resumes. A resume states verifiable experience and results. Tailoring means choosing relevant facts, not inventing credentials.

Document styles. Headings, spacing, and page structure should be consistent. Word styles make long documents easier to revise.

Spreadsheet reasoning. Separate labels, input cells, formulas, and checks. For Price in B2 and Quantity in C2, Total in D2 is =B2*C2.

Presentations and databases. Slides need one main idea each. Access tables need clear keys and relationships before forms or reports.

Worked example

Worked example: A resume bullet might change from “Did office work” to “Organized 120 client records in a consistent filing system,” but only if the client confirms the number and work. A matching cover letter gives context, not a duplicate list of every bullet.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A client says to add an unearned certificate to improve a resume. How do you respond?

Model answer: Do not add it. Offer to emphasize real training, projects, and relevant skills instead.

Client situation

A client needs a resume, cover letter, and clean Office documents.

Ask before you begin

• What job posting or audience is the material for?

• What dates, titles, accomplishments, and education are verified?

• Which file format and editing access does the client need?

• Are there existing documents whose content must be preserved?

Do the job step by step

1. Interview the client for factual experience and measurable results; never invent credentials.

2. Make a master fact sheet with titles, employers, dates, skills, and approved wording.

3. Tailor the resume to the job using truthful relevant evidence and clear section headings.

4. Draft a cover letter that names the role, connects two or three real examples, and closes with a specific interest.

5. Format in Word or another agreed tool using styles rather than repeated manual spacing.

6. For Excel, define column meanings, use formulas carefully, and verify totals against sample inputs.

7. For PowerPoint, give each slide one main idea and check projection legibility. For Access, define tables, keys, and relationships before forms or reports.

8. Proofread facts, dates, spelling, links, page breaks, and PDF export before delivery.

Check your work

• No fabricated achievements or unexplained date changes.

• Text remains readable in Word and exported PDF.

• A resume can be scanned quickly for relevant experience.

• Spreadsheet formulas use the intended cells and recalculate.

• The editable file opens correctly.

Practice assignment

Create a fictional administrative assistant resume, one-page cover letter, a Word event memo, a five-row Excel expense tracker, and a three-slide introduction. Verify every number and label.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 5 Research & Writing

Research assistance, proofreading, editing, citations, and structured writing

What this service teaches

Question and scope. Turn “research this topic” into a clear question with audience, date range, depth, and output format.

Source evaluation. Check who produced a source, when, why, and whether it directly supports the claim.

Synthesis. Compare sources and explain what they collectively show rather than stacking copied excerpts.

Editing levels. Proofreading fixes surface errors. Copyediting improves consistency and clarity. Structural editing changes organization while preserving the author’s intent.

Worked example

Worked example: To research community gardens, ask whether the client wants startup steps, costs, or benefits. Gather sources for that question. In a source log, record each claim beside a URL or publication detail. Draft the summary in your own words and verify each citation.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: You find a persuasive article with no date or author. Can it be your only source for a factual claim?

Model answer: It may be a lead, but verify the claim with a more traceable and reliable source before relying on it.

Client situation

A client needs a short, sourced overview and an edited draft.

Ask before you begin

• What exact question must the research answer?

• Who is the reader, and how long should the result be?

• Which citation style, source types, and deadline are required?

• Is the job research support, editing, or writing from scratch?

Do the job step by step

1. Turn the broad request into a narrow research question and a list of subquestions.

2. Collect reliable sources and record author, title, date, URL or publication details, and the claim each supports.

3. Distinguish fact, interpretation, and recommendation in your notes.

4. Outline the answer before drafting; connect each main claim to evidence.

5. Paraphrase in your own words and cite the source. Quote sparingly and accurately.

6. Edit for structure, clarity, grammar, tone, and the client’s intended voice. Track major changes.

7. Check each citation against the source and verify numbers, names, and links.

8. Deliver clean copy plus the agreed source list or edit notes.

Check your work

• The answer actually addresses the question.

• No source is invented; citations point to the claim they support.

• Borrowed wording is quoted or properly paraphrased.

• The edited text preserves the author’s meaning.

• The client can identify what changed.

Practice assignment

Research a fictional community garden proposal using three real public sources. Write a one-page summary with source notes, then edit a rough paragraph without changing its meaning.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 6 Clerical Support

Typing, data entry, organization, forms, and bookkeeping support

What this service teaches

Data accuracy. Transcribe from a defined source. Decide formats for dates, amounts, names, and categories before entering a large batch.

Reconciliation. Compare counts and totals to the original records. A mismatch is a question to investigate, not a number to force.

Bookkeeping support boundary. Recording and organizing client-approved transactions is different from making tax or accounting judgments.

Confidentiality. Use private storage and minimum necessary access; avoid copying client data into public examples.

Worked example

Worked example: Twenty receipts total $480 on the source cover sheet. After entry, the spreadsheet totals $505. Find the $25 duplicate by sorting date, vendor, and amount. Record the correction and preserve the original receipt.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A receipt has an unreadable vendor. Should you invent the most likely name?

Model answer: No. Flag the entry as unclear and ask the client or check another authorized source.

Client situation

A client has receipts and contacts that must be organized.

Ask before you begin

• What records are being handled, and how sensitive are they?

• What folder or spreadsheet structure does the client already use?

• Who approves corrections to ambiguous entries?

• Does bookkeeping mean data organization or a separately agreed accounting task?

Do the job step by step

1. Confirm scope and access. Use the least access needed and a private workspace.

2. Make a consistent naming and data-entry guide: dates, categories, currency, and source references.

3. Enter a small batch first; compare it with originals and get approval of the format.

4. Process the remaining records in batches, preserving originals and an exception list.

5. For receipts, record transaction date, vendor, amount, category supplied or approved by client, and document location.

6. Reconcile counts and totals against the source documents. Investigate differences; never force totals to match.

7. Flag missing or duplicate records and ask the client instead of guessing.

8. Deliver organized files, an exceptions log, and a summary of work performed.

Check your work

• Every record traces back to a source.

• Duplicate and missing items are marked.

• Totals match the entered records and are independently checked.

• Private data is shared only with authorized people.

• Tax, legal, and accounting conclusions are referred to the appropriate qualified professional.

Practice assignment

Use 20 fictional receipts. Enter them in a spreadsheet, calculate category totals, plant one duplicate deliberately, then find and document it.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 7 Event Planning

Timelines, guest details, vendor coordination, and event materials

What this service teaches

Critical path. Some tasks depend on others: venue and date must be confirmed before invitations can be final.

Budget tracking. Estimate each category, record quoted and actual costs separately, and keep a contingency for changes.

Run of show. A minute-by-minute or segment-by-segment plan states the time, action, owner, and location.

Contingencies. Identify likely disruptions and who can approve a substitute or change.

Worked example

Worked example: For a 2–5 PM celebration, set guest arrival at 1:45, welcome at 2:10, activity at 2:30, refreshments at 3:15, and closeout by 5. Assign one person to each transition and confirm venue access for setup and cleanup.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: Invitations are ready, but the venue has not confirmed the date. What is the next step?

Model answer: Hold distribution until the venue and date are confirmed; otherwise guests may receive incorrect information.

Client situation

A family requests planning support for a celebration.

Ask before you begin

• What is the date, venue, guest count, budget, and decision maker?

• Which tasks are yours versus the client’s or vendors’ responsibilities?

• Are accessibility, weather, travel, and dietary needs relevant?

• What changes are possible if a vendor cancels?

Do the job step by step

1. Write an event brief and confirm the budget and priorities.

2. Create a master timeline with decision deadlines, setup, event flow, and cleanup.

3. Make a guest and vendor contact list with only necessary information.

4. Request written quotes from vendors; record pricing, deadlines, and terms before the client chooses.

5. Build a run-of-show with times, owners, locations, and backup contacts.

6. Prepare approved invitations, signs, programs, and checklists with matching details.

7. Confirm details with the client and vendors near the event date. Record changes in one master version.

8. After the event, collect final documents and a short lessons-learned note.

Check your work

• Every major task has an owner and due date.

• Venue, times, guest details, and materials agree.

• Vendor commitments are confirmed, not assumed.

• A backup plan covers key dependencies.

• Personal guest information is handled privately.

Practice assignment

Plan a fictional 30-person birthday celebration. Make a budget, six-week timeline, run-of-show, vendor comparison, and two backup plans.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 8 Social Media & Digital Support

Graphics, page materials, content layouts, and online support

What this service teaches

Content strategy. Choose a purpose for each post: inform, explain, show proof, invite conversation, or announce.

Platform format. Text length, image crop, and reading behavior differ across channels. Review the actual preview.

Approval and scheduling. A content calendar tracks draft, reviewed, approved, scheduled, and published states.

Measurement. Track a small number of outcomes tied to the goal, such as link clicks or inquiries, rather than treating every like as a sale.

Worked example

Worked example: A cafe announces a new drink. Post one clear photo with its name, availability, and a working contact or location link. A second post shows preparation. Avoid repeating the same announcement eight times.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A draft post includes a customer photo but nobody has confirmed permission. Can you publish?

Model answer: No. Get permission or replace the photo with approved imagery before publishing.

Client situation

A client needs a month of posts for a new service.

Ask before you begin

• Which platform and audience are you designing for?

• What goal does each post serve?

• Who approves claims, photos, tags, and account access?

• Is the engagement work limited to drafts or does it include publishing and replies?

Do the job step by step

1. Collect the brand voice, visual assets, goals, and any approved offers.

2. Make a content calendar with date, platform, topic, format, caption, asset, and approval state.

3. Draft useful and varied posts instead of repeating the same sales message.

4. Design graphics with readable text and dimensions suited to the platform.

5. Check factual claims, links, spelling, permissions, and accessibility text.

6. Send a batch for approval; track revisions and final approved versions.

7. If publishing is in scope, use authorized access and verify the live post after scheduling.

8. Report what was published and simple results the client actually asked to track.

Check your work

• No unapproved personal images or claims.

• Caption and graphic say the same thing.

• Links and contact paths work.

• Text remains legible on a phone.

• Approval and publication status are recorded.

Practice assignment

Create a fictional four-week calendar with eight posts for Muffins N Mocha: two announcements, two helpful tips, two behind-the-scenes stories, and two community posts.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 9 Business Cards

Print and digital card layouts

What this service teaches

Information hierarchy. Name or business, role, and a reliable way to contact the person should be easy to read instantly.

Physical scale. Zooming in on screen hides tiny text. Print a proof at actual size.

Bleed and safe zone. Artwork may extend into bleed; text and logos should remain inside the printer’s safe area.

QR codes. A QR code is useful only when its destination is correct and the printed code scans at actual size.

Worked example

Worked example: On a 3.5 × 2 inch card, put the logo and business name on the front. On the back, place the owner name, title, phone, email, and one website or QR code with breathing room. Compare two versions by printing them at 100% scale.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: A QR code scans on screen but not on the printed proof. What should you check?

Model answer: Check its printed size, contrast, quiet space, resolution, and destination; print and scan another proof.

Client situation

A client wants a polished two-sided business card.

Ask before you begin

• What exact name, title, phone, email, website, and social links belong on it?

• What printer specification, card size, bleed, and safe margin apply?

• Does the client want a QR code, and what destination should it open?

• Which logo version and brand colors are approved?

Do the job step by step

1. Collect contact text in writing and verify every character.

2. Get the printer template or specifications before creating the artboard.

3. Sketch front and back with clear hierarchy; keep the most useful information prominent.

4. Use high-quality logo assets and readable type at actual card size.

5. Leave the printer’s required bleed and safe area; avoid tiny text near trim.

6. If adding a QR code, generate it for the final URL and scan-test it on a phone.

7. Export a proof for the client; ask them to approve contact details explicitly.

8. Export print-ready and digital versions in the formats requested by the printer and client.

Check your work

• All contact details are accurate.

• Card is readable at 100% physical size.

• Bleed, margins, and color format match the chosen printer’s requirements.

• QR destination works and remains useful.

• Client approved the proof before print files were released.

Practice assignment

Design a fictional two-sided business card for a bookshop. Make two layouts, print them at actual size, compare legibility, and document the better choice.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 10 Vocal & Special Occasion Services

Singing and creative contributions to special events

What this service teaches

Set design. Choose songs or original material that fit the event, audience, duration, and performer’s range.

Rehearsal. Time the full set, including introductions and transitions, not only individual songs.

Sound setup. Confirm microphone, accompaniment, power, monitor, and a backup audio option.

Professional coordination. A clear contact person, arrival time, sound check, and performance slot prevent surprises.

Worked example

Worked example: A 15-minute set might include a 1-minute introduction, three 4-minute songs, and 2 minutes for transitions. Rehearse the actual sequence, then adjust so the set fits without rushing.

Check your understanding

Knowledge check: The venue says it has a microphone but has not confirmed speakers or a sound technician. Is the setup complete?

Model answer: No. Confirm the full signal path, operator, sound-check time, and backup before relying on the setup.

Client situation

A client requests a vocal performance for a celebration.

Ask before you begin

• What event, date, venue, audience, and exact performance slot?

• How long is the set, and which songs or original pieces are requested?

• Who supplies sound equipment and handles setup or a sound check?

• What are the arrival time, travel needs, dress expectations, and backup plan?

Do the job step by step

1. Discuss the event’s tone and agree on a setlist or type of performance.

2. Confirm song versions, duration, accompaniment, and any permissions needed for recorded or published use.

3. Write a simple performance agreement with schedule, scope, fee, cancellation terms, and equipment responsibilities.

4. Rehearse transitions and time the complete set, including introductions.

5. Check the microphone, backing track or accompanist, monitoring, and file backup before the event.

6. Arrive at the agreed time, sound-check, and coordinate with the event contact.

7. Perform the agreed set and adapt to reasonable timing changes through the contact person.

8. Afterward, provide any agreed recording or follow-up only with permission from everyone involved.

Check your work

• Set length and song choices match the agreement.

• Equipment and backup audio are tested.

• Venue contact knows the arrival and performance times.

• Any recording or promotional use has permission.

• The service remains within the performer’s comfortable and safe capability.

Practice assignment

Plan a fictional 15-minute celebration set. Write a setlist with timings, a sound-check checklist, one backup song, and a concise confirmation message.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Individual service practice labs

Use the relevant full lesson first. These short labs help you practice the specific items in the Services menu. Use fictional clients and verify every detail with an approved brief before real delivery.

Website or digital solution. Sketch the visitor’s path; build the pages and forms; test phone and desktop layouts, links, and accessibility; prepare a launch and rollback checklist.

Flyer, poster, or banner. Rank headline, date, place, and action; design to the requested dimensions; proof against source text; export a size-correct review and print file.

Business card. Set printer size and bleed; place approved logo and contact details; proof at actual size and scan QR code; release print file after approval.

Church program. Confirm service order and names with the organizer; create a readable page sequence; proof all scripture references and participant names; review the final fold or binding order.

Memorial program. Request approved biography, photos, and service order; handle family wording with care; verify dates and names with one approver; export a print proof before final files.

Resume or cover letter. Collect a truthful job history and target posting; choose relevant accomplishments; tailor the letter; check dates, claims, links, and PDF reading order.

Bookkeeping support. Define the period and categories; enter only source-backed transactions; reconcile totals to statements; flag unresolved items for the client or qualified accountant.

Research or editing. Agree on question, audience, and source standard; gather and cite sources; separate facts from interpretation; proof the final text against the brief.

Microsoft Word. Set styles and page layout; insert headings, tables, and references as needed; check navigation and page breaks; deliver editable and PDF copies.

Microsoft Excel. Define columns and input rules; build formulas on sample records; test edge cases and totals; document how the client should update the sheet.

Microsoft PowerPoint. Outline one point per slide; apply consistent type and contrast; add speaker notes if requested; test on a projected or full-screen view.

Microsoft Access. Draw tables and keys first; enter sample records; build a query, form, and report; test relationships, validation, and backup.

Data entry. Agree on source, fields, and duplicate rules; enter a small batch; compare a sample to originals; correct exceptions and log completion.

Clerical or administrative support. Make an authorized task list; organize files or communications; track deadlines and open questions; hand back a status summary.

Event planning. Write the event goal, budget, and run of show; confirm vendors and responsibilities; rehearse timing and contingencies; close with a final checklist.

Branding or design. Interview for audience and positioning; sketch distinct directions; test in real sizes and contexts; provide an approved asset kit and usage notes.

Social media or digital support. Choose audience, channel, and goal; draft a small content calendar; verify permissions and claims; test links, schedule, and measure results.

Vocal or special occasion service. Agree on songs, duration, and event tone; rehearse the timed set; confirm sound and arrival details; prepare a backup plan.

Custom project. Write the outcome and deliverables in plain language; identify skills and boundaries; prototype a small sample; quote and schedule only after scope is agreed.

Final practice review

Before using a practice sample as portfolio evidence, identify it as a fictional concept. Do not imply a pretend client ordered it. For real work, record approval and the scope delivered.

Self-assessment for every lesson

• I asked enough questions to define the result.

• I completed the steps in order and kept source materials organized.

• I can explain why I made the key choices.

• I ran the category checklist and corrected any failures.

• I can hand the final files to another person without a long explanation.

Suggested order of study

Start with Business Cards and Branding & Creative for visual fundamentals. Continue with Career & Office, Research & Writing, and Clerical Support. Then practice Social Media & Digital Support and Event Planning. Tackle Website Design and Business Tools with the coding classroom beside you. Practice Vocal & Special Occasion Services with a timed rehearsal.

Client handoff message template

Hello [Name], the approved [deliverable] is ready. Included: [files and formats]. I checked [key items]. Please download and review by [date]. If a file does not open or a factual detail needs correction, reply with the filename and the issue. Thank you, Templar.

A note about your current site

These ten lessons use the service categories currently presented on S3LFM@DE Solutions. They do not replace your live website or change its Services section. Keep orders paused until you choose to open your business.

title: Service Workflow Workbook
content:
S3LFM@DE Solutions Service Workflow Workbook

A step-by-step practice manual for Templar Hughes-Bryant. This workbook covers the ten current service categories on your website. Each lesson shows how to define the job, collect the right materials, make a draft, check quality, and deliver. Complete the practice project for each category before accepting a similar paid job.

Use fictional names and data in practice. Keep this manual beside your coding classroom. When the business is ready to open, confirm each client’s scope, fee, timeline, revision allowance, and required materials in writing before work begins. Your current public status keeps orders paused until you decide to open.

How to use the classroom

1. Read the client brief and workflow for one service category.

2. Complete its practice project using fictional information.

3. Run its quality checklist and revise what fails.

4. Save a clean sample, the editable source, and a short note on what you learned.

5. Repeat a module when the practice sample does not yet meet your standard.

Universal client workflow

1. Receive an inquiry and ask what outcome the client needs. Do not guess at the deliverable.

2. Write a short brief: audience, content, size or format, deadline, brand assets, accessibility needs, and who approves.

3. Define scope: exact files or tasks, number of concepts, revisions, exclusions, and price or estimate.

4. Confirm that the client has permission to supply photos, logos, text, and data. Store their files in a private project folder.

5. Make a first draft, then compare it against the brief before sharing.

6. Ask for consolidated feedback and record each requested change. Separate fixes from new scope.

7. Perform a final content, function, accessibility, and file-format check.

8. Deliver the agreed files with clear filenames and a short handoff note. Preserve a backup and close the project record.

Reusable project folder

Client_Project/

01_Brief/

02_Source_Files/

03_Drafts/

04_Review_Notes/

05_Final_Delivery/

Naming example: ClientName_Flyer_v01.pdf for a draft and ClientName_Flyer_FINAL.pdf for approved delivery. Avoid naming a draft FINAL before approval.

Lesson 1 Website Design

Responsive websites and digital experiences

Client situation

A small business wants a five-page site that visitors can use on a phone.

Ask before you begin

• What pages, actions, and content are required?

• Who owns the domain and hosting account?

• Is there an existing logo, brand guide, privacy notice, and approved copy?

• Does the site need accounts, payments, booking, or a database? These change scope substantially.

Do the job step by step

1. Make a page list and a simple navigation map: Home, About, Services, Portfolio, Contact.

2. Collect approved text, photos, logo files, contact links, and any required policy text. Record missing items.

3. Sketch mobile and desktop layouts with headings, calls to action, and clear reading order.

4. Build semantic HTML and responsive CSS. Add JavaScript only for behavior the site needs.

5. Check every link, form, button, image, and path. Do not label a form as working until messages actually arrive.

6. Test narrow and wide screens, keyboard navigation, readable contrast, image alt text, and loading speed.

7. Review with the client on a private preview. Record requested changes and obtain approval.

8. Make a backup, publish to the agreed hosting account, then retest the live URL and document the handoff.

Check your work

• Five page links work in both directions.

• No placeholder wording or broken images remain.

• Mobile view has no horizontal overflow.

• Forms and dynamic features are tested end to end, or clearly labeled as demos.

• Client receives ownership and maintenance information for accounts and files.

Practice assignment

Build a fictional three-page site for Muffins N Mocha: Home, Menu, Contact. Use a working navigation menu, a responsive layout, and a practice-only contact form that clearly says it does not send messages.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 2 Branding & Creative

Flyers, banners, invitations, advertisements, and social graphics

Client situation

A client requests a church program and a matching flyer for an event.

Ask before you begin

• What exact words, date, time, location, names, and spelling must appear?

• What is the intended print or digital size?

• Are photos, logos, and colors approved and high enough quality?

• What is the order of importance: headline, event details, call to action?

Do the job step by step

1. Ask for the content in writing and mark anything missing; verify names and dates with the client.

2. Create a visual hierarchy so a reader notices the main message first.

3. Choose two readable typefaces or a restrained type system and a consistent palette.

4. Set the correct page size and safe margins before designing. Allow space for printer trimming when requested.

5. Place content and images. Check licensing or the client’s permission to use supplied imagery.

6. Proofread each line against the approved source, including phone, address, time zone, and website.

7. Export a review PDF or image, gather consolidated feedback, revise, and request final approval.

8. Export the agreed print and digital formats; keep editable source files organized.

Check your work

• All mandatory information is present and legible at intended size.

• No text sits too close to the trim edge.

• Photos are sharp and not stretched.

• Spelling and dates match the approved brief.

• Final files have descriptive names and the agreed dimensions.

Practice assignment

Design a fictional two-page church program and a matching event flyer. Make a content checklist before opening the design tool. Proofread from bottom to top after the first draft.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 3 Business Tools

Custom forms, workflows, customer-facing tools, and automation concepts

Client situation

A small organization wants a request form and a simple status tracker.

Ask before you begin

• What information is truly necessary?

• Who may see or edit each record?

• Which steps happen after submission, and who owns each step?

• What must happen when a form fails or a duplicate is submitted?

Do the job step by step

1. Map the current process as intake, review, decision, work, and closeout.

2. List fields with their purpose; remove unnecessary sensitive data.

3. Sketch the form and status states before building. Define required fields and helpful error text.

4. Build a prototype with fictional records. Keep secrets and privileged actions on a server, never in public HTML.

5. Test empty input, invalid input, long input, duplicate submission, and interrupted connection.

6. Check keyboard use, labels, readable feedback, and privacy of each view.

7. Demonstrate the process to the client and document who maintains it.

8. Deliver the agreed tool plus a one-page usage guide and a backup plan.

Check your work

• Every field has a clear label and purpose.

• Errors tell the user what to fix without erasing their work.

• Unauthorized users cannot see or change private records.

• The workflow has an owner for each step.

• The client can use and maintain the tool after handoff.

Practice assignment

Build a practice request tracker using five fictional entries and statuses New, Reviewing, Waiting, In Progress, and Complete. Write the rules for moving between statuses.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 4 Career & Office

Resumes, cover letters, bios, and Microsoft Office work

Client situation

A client needs a resume, cover letter, and clean Office documents.

Ask before you begin

• What job posting or audience is the material for?

• What dates, titles, accomplishments, and education are verified?

• Which file format and editing access does the client need?

• Are there existing documents whose content must be preserved?

Do the job step by step

1. Interview the client for factual experience and measurable results; never invent credentials.

2. Make a master fact sheet with titles, employers, dates, skills, and approved wording.

3. Tailor the resume to the job using truthful relevant evidence and clear section headings.

4. Draft a cover letter that names the role, connects two or three real examples, and closes with a specific interest.

5. Format in Word or another agreed tool using styles rather than repeated manual spacing.

6. For Excel, define column meanings, use formulas carefully, and verify totals against sample inputs.

7. For PowerPoint, give each slide one main idea and check projection legibility. For Access, define tables, keys, and relationships before forms or reports.

8. Proofread facts, dates, spelling, links, page breaks, and PDF export before delivery.

Check your work

• No fabricated achievements or unexplained date changes.

• Text remains readable in Word and exported PDF.

• A resume can be scanned quickly for relevant experience.

• Spreadsheet formulas use the intended cells and recalculate.

• The editable file opens correctly.

Practice assignment

Create a fictional administrative assistant resume, one-page cover letter, a Word event memo, a five-row Excel expense tracker, and a three-slide introduction. Verify every number and label.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 5 Research & Writing

Research assistance, proofreading, editing, citations, and structured writing

Client situation

A client needs a short, sourced overview and an edited draft.

Ask before you begin

• What exact question must the research answer?

• Who is the reader, and how long should the result be?

• Which citation style, source types, and deadline are required?

• Is the job research support, editing, or writing from scratch?

Do the job step by step

1. Turn the broad request into a narrow research question and a list of subquestions.

2. Collect reliable sources and record author, title, date, URL or publication details, and the claim each supports.

3. Distinguish fact, interpretation, and recommendation in your notes.

4. Outline the answer before drafting; connect each main claim to evidence.

5. Paraphrase in your own words and cite the source. Quote sparingly and accurately.

6. Edit for structure, clarity, grammar, tone, and the client’s intended voice. Track major changes.

7. Check each citation against the source and verify numbers, names, and links.

8. Deliver clean copy plus the agreed source list or edit notes.

Check your work

• The answer actually addresses the question.

• No source is invented; citations point to the claim they support.

• Borrowed wording is quoted or properly paraphrased.

• The edited text preserves the author’s meaning.

• The client can identify what changed.

Practice assignment

Research a fictional community garden proposal using three real public sources. Write a one-page summary with source notes, then edit a rough paragraph without changing its meaning.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Lesson 6 Clerical Support

Typing, data entry, organization, forms, and bookkeeping support

Client situation

A client has receipts and contacts that must be organized.

Ask before you begin

• What records are being handled, and how sensitive are they?

• What folder or spreadsheet structure does the client already use?

• Who approves corrections to ambiguous entries?

• Does bookkeeping mean data organization or a separately agreed accounting task?

Do the job step by step

1. Confirm scope and access. Use the least access needed and a private workspace.

2. Make a consistent naming and data-entry guide: dates, categories, currency, and source references.

3. Enter a small batch first; compare it with originals and get approval of the format.

4. Process the remaining records in batches, preserving originals and an exception list.

5. For receipts, record transaction date, vendor, amount, category supplied or approved by client, and document location.

6. Reconcile counts and totals against the source documents. Investigate differences; never force totals to match.

7. Flag missing or duplicate records and ask the client instead of guessing.

8. Deliver organized files, an exceptions log, and a summary of work performed.

Check your work

• Every record traces back to a source.

• Duplicate and missing items are marked.

• Totals match the entered records and are independently checked.

• Private data is shared only with authorized people.

• Tax, legal, and accounting conclusions are referred to the appropriate qualified professional.

Practice assignment

Use 20 fictional receipts. Enter them in a spreadsheet, calculate category totals, plant one duplicate deliberately, then find and document it.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

• Any recording or promotional use has permission.

• The service remains within the performer’s comfortable and safe capability.

Practice assignment

Plan a fictional 15-minute celebration set. Write a setlist with timings, a sound-check checklist, one backup song, and a concise confirmation message.

What to save

Brief, working source, review copy, final sample, quality checklist, and a short note describing what you would improve next time.

Final practice review

Before using a practice sample as portfolio evidence, identify it as a fictional concept. Do not imply a pretend client ordered it. For real work, record approval and the scope delivered.

Self-assessment for every lesson

• I asked enough questions to define the result.

• I completed the steps in order and kept source materials organized.

• I can explain why I made the key choices.

• I ran the category checklist and corrected any failures.

• I can hand the final files to another person without a long explanation.

Suggested order of study

Start with Business Cards and Branding & Creative for visual fundamentals. Continue with Career & Office, Research & Writing, and Clerical Support. Then practice Social Media & Digital Support and Event Planning. Tackle Website Design and Business Tools with the coding classroom beside you. Practice Vocal & Special Occasion Services with a timed rehearsal.

Client handoff message template

Hello [Name], the approved [deliverable] is ready. Included: [files and formats]. I checked [key items]. Please download and review by [date]. If a file does not open or a factual detail needs correction, reply with the filename and the issue. Thank you, Templar.

A note about your current site

These ten lessons use the service categories currently presented on S3LFM@DE Solutions. They do not replace your live website or change its Services section. Keep orders paused until you choose to open your business.

title: Technical Troubleshooting Classroom 100 Lessons
content:
Technical Troubleshooting Classroom

100 common computer problems with step by step fixes

Prepared for Templar Hughes Bryant

How to use your classroom

Find the lesson matching the problem you actually see. Each lesson names the symptom, explains likely causes, gives numbered actions, describes what should appear, and shows how to test the result. These are first troubleshooting steps; some failures need a technician or the service provider.

Work through one step at a time. After the action, read “What you should see.” If your screen differs, stop there and write down the message or show that screen when asking for help. Do not continue just because the next step is printed.

The steps primarily use Windows 11, desktop Microsoft Word and Excel, Chrome, and Gmail in a browser. Word and Excel lessons apply only when those apps are available. Labels can differ by version. For Windows 10, Devices replaces Bluetooth & devices in many paths; Privacy replaces Privacy & security, and Update & Security contains Windows Update.

Before restarting or ending an app, save any work you can. Before testing a document change, save a copy. A plus sign in a keyboard shortcut means hold the first key while pressing the others. The Windows key has the Windows logo.

The original 50 lessons have been rewritten with more detail. Lessons 51 through 100 add new browser, display, Word, Excel, and email problems. This workbook contains 100 lessons in total; your separate original Chrome lesson remains a worked example.

Lesson guide 1 to 25

14. Airplane mode blocks connections

15. The wrong Wi-Fi network is selected

16. Wi-Fi password is rejected

17. Internet drops repeatedly

18. A VPN makes a site fail

19. A wired connection is not working

20. Wi-Fi is unavailable or will not reconnect

Lesson guide 26 to 50

28. A USB drive does not appear

30. A file is too large to email

32. Sound plays through the wrong device

34. Camera shows a black picture

35. Bluetooth headphones will not connect

36. A printer is offline

37. A print job is stuck

38. The wrong printer is selected

39. Mouse pointer feels too fast

40. Keyboard types unexpected characters

41. An app is frozen

42. The computer is slow after startup

43. Windows Update is stuck

44. A program will not open

45. You forgot a website password

46. A password reset email does not arrive

47. An account says the password is wrong

48. A suspicious pop-up says the PC is infected

49. A Windows notification keeps appearing

50. Windows shows the wrong date or time

Lesson guide 51 to 75

51. Chrome says it needs an update

52. You closed a browser tab by mistake

53. A website keeps asking you to sign in

54. A website sends unwanted notifications

55. A legitimate pop-up window is blocked

56. A video on a webpage has no sound

57. A PDF opens in Chrome when you wanted to save it

58. A webpage form lost your typed information

59. Chrome saved the wrong password

60. A page says your connection is not private

61. Everything on the screen is too small

62. The screen is too dim

63. The picture looks stretched or blurry

64. A second monitor shows no picture

65. The desktop appears on the wrong monitor

66. The screen is sideways

67. The mouse stops responding

68. The laptop touchpad does not move the pointer

69. The number keypad will not type numbers

70. A USB accessory works poorly through a hub

71. Word will not let you edit a downloaded document

72. Word opens a document as read only

73. Word changes disappeared after a crash

74. Word has an unwanted blank page

75. Dots and paragraph symbols appear in Word

Lesson guide 76 to 100

76. Pasted text has the wrong font and spacing

77. Word text is too tiny to read

78. A paragraph has too much space after it

79. Word underlines words in the wrong language

80. Word says Unlicensed Product

81. Excel displays hash marks instead of a number

82. Excel shows formulas instead of results

83. Excel totals do not change after editing

84. Excel ignores numbers in a sum

85. Excel shows DIV zero in a formula

86. Excel shows a REF error

87. Excel shows a NAME error

88. Excel prints a sheet across too many pages

89. Excel rows or columns seem missing

90. Scrolling in Excel moves the sheet instead of the cell

91. An expected email is missing

92. Gmail says storage is full

94. An attachment never finishes uploading

95. You cannot find the attachment in an email

96. Gmail opened the wrong account

97. An email was deleted accidentally

98. Gmail appears frozen or shows a temporary error

99. A legitimate sender keeps going to Spam

100. You sent the wrong email and want to stop it

Chrome and websites

Lesson 1 Search engine changes back by itself

What the problem means

An extension or installed program may be changing Chrome settings again.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open Google Chrome. What you should see: A browser window appears.

2. Click the three dots in the upper right corner. What you should see: The Chrome menu opens.

3. Click Settings. What you should see: A Settings tab opens.

4. Click Search engine in the Settings menu. What you should see: The Search engine page appears.

5. Read the current search engine name. Write it down before changing it. What you should see: You have a record of the original choice.

6. Click Change beside the current choice. What you should see: A list of search engines opens.

7. Select the engine you prefer and confirm if asked. What you should see: The selected name appears on the Settings page.

8. Close Chrome, reopen it, and try a new search from the long address bar at the top. What you should see: The search uses your chosen engine.

9. If it changes back, click the three dots, then Extensions, then Manage extensions. What you should see: A list of installed extensions appears.

10. Switch off one search-related extension you recognize. Set the engine again and retry. What you should see: You can compare behavior with that extension off.

Check whether the fix worked

The setting stays saved after reopening Chrome; record the extension involved if it changes only when switched on.

If it still does not work

If the choice is locked or the extension is managed, record the message and ask the computer administrator. Do not keep changing unrelated settings.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 2 Chrome opens unwanted pages at startup

What the problem means

A startup page setting may tell Chrome to reopen an old site.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open Google Chrome. What you should see: A browser window appears.

2. Click the three dots in the upper right corner. What you should see: The Chrome menu opens.

3. Click Settings. What you should see: A Settings tab opens.

4. Click On startup in the Settings menu. What you should see: The On startup page appears.

5. Read the selected startup option. What you should see: You can see whether Chrome restores tabs or opens specific pages.

6. Select Open the New Tab page. What you should see: The selection dot moves beside that option.

7. Click the three dots, then Exit. Reopen Chrome. What you should see: A new tab should open instead of the unwanted page.

Check whether the fix worked

Chrome starts on the page you chose.

If it still does not work

If the unwanted page returns, inspect extensions as in Lesson 1.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 3 A website will not load

What the problem means

The problem may belong to one page, Chrome, or the connection.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the long address bar at the top of Chrome. Check the spelling of the website address. What you should see: You can see the actual address you are visiting.

2. Hold Ctrl and press R to reload. What you should see: The page tries to load again.

3. Click the plus sign beside the tabs to open a new tab. What you should see: A blank tab opens.

4. Type the address of a different familiar website and press Enter. What you should see: You find out whether another site can load.

5. Hold Ctrl and Shift, then press N. What you should see: A dark Incognito window opens.

6. Type the original site address there and press Enter. What you should see: You can compare the same site in a separate browser session.

Check whether the fix worked

Record which sites work and whether Incognito changes the result.

If it still does not work

If all sites fail, go to the internet lessons. If only one fails, record its error and try again later.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 4 A page keeps showing an old version

What the problem means

Chrome may be showing stored page data.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open the page showing old content. What you should see: You can see the outdated information.

2. Hold Ctrl and press R. What you should see: Chrome reloads the page.

3. If unchanged, hold Ctrl and Shift and press R. What you should see: Chrome requests a fresh page copy.

4. Close that tab with its X, then open the site again in a new tab. What you should see: The page is loaded in a new tab.

Check whether the fix worked

The page shows its current content; if not, the site itself may not have updated.

If it still does not work

If it still shows the old version, the website or its server cache may not have updated. Do not erase all browser data first.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 5 Chrome says Aw Snap

What the problem means

A tab crashed, often because of a temporary page or memory problem.

Fix it one step at a time

1. On the Aw Snap page, click Reload. What you should see: Chrome attempts to reopen the page.

2. Close unused tabs by clicking their tab X buttons. What you should see: Fewer pages remain open.

3. Save work in other apps before closing them. What you should see: Your documents are preserved.

4. Click Chrome’s three dots, then Exit. What you should see: The browser closes.

5. Open Chrome and visit the same page. What you should see: You can check whether the crash repeats.

Check whether the fix worked

The page stays open without crashing.

If it still does not work

If it crashes repeatedly on only one site, record the address and error. If many sites crash, check Chrome updates in Lesson 51.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 6 Chrome is unusually slow

What the problem means

Too many tabs, extensions, or background apps can consume memory.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the X on browser tabs you are finished using. What you should see: The tab count decreases.

2. Save work in other open programs. What you should see: You can close those apps without losing work.

3. Close unused apps with the X in each app window. What you should see: Fewer apps are running.

4. Return to Chrome and reload the slow page with Ctrl and R. What you should see: You can compare its response time.

5. Try a different simple website. What you should see: You can tell whether the slowdown belongs to one page.

Check whether the fix worked

Pages respond faster; note if one particular page remains slow.

If it still does not work

If the entire computer is slow, see the Windows startup lesson. Record when the slowdown begins.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 7 A Chrome extension changes pages

What the problem means

An extension can affect searches or page loading.

Fix it one step at a time

1. In Chrome, click the three dots in the upper right. What you should see: The browser menu opens.

2. Click Extensions, then Manage extensions. What you should see: Installed extensions appear as cards.

3. Read each name and locate the extension you suspect. What you should see: You know which switch you will change.

4. Click that extension’s on and off switch once to turn it off. What you should see: Its switch appears off.

5. Reload the affected page with Ctrl and R. What you should see: You can test the change.

6. If it made no difference, turn that extension back on. What you should see: The original extension setting is restored.

Check whether the fix worked

The behavior changes only while a specific extension is off.

If it still does not work

Test one extension at a time. If a specific extension causes the problem, check its publisher and settings before deciding whether to remove it.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 8 Chrome will not download a file

What the problem means

The site, destination, or a safety warning may be involved.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Press Ctrl+J. For a shortcut with a plus sign, hold the first key while pressing the next, then release them. What you should see: Chrome’s Downloads page opens.

2. Read the message beside the failed file. What you should see: You know whether the issue is a network error, blocked file, or interrupted download.

3. Open another familiar website in a new tab. What you should see: You can confirm the internet connection works.

4. If the file is from a trusted source and only the download was interrupted, click Retry if shown. What you should see: Chrome attempts the download again.

5. When finished, click Show in folder. What you should see: File Explorer displays the downloaded file.

Check whether the fix worked

The file appears in Downloads; never bypass a warning for an unknown file.

If it still does not work

Do not bypass a security warning for an unknown file. Record the exact download error if Retry fails.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 9 A website cannot use the microphone

What the problem means

The site or Windows may lack microphone permission.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open the trusted website that needs your microphone. What you should see: Its address is visible at the top of Chrome.

2. Click the controls icon immediately to the left of the website address. What you should see: A small site information panel opens.

3. Click Site settings. What you should see: Permissions for that site open.

4. Find Microphone and select Allow if you want this site to use it. What you should see: The permission shows Allow.

5. Return to the website tab and reload it. What you should see: The updated permission takes effect.

6. Click the site’s microphone test or recording button and speak. What you should see: The site should show an audio level or recording.

Check whether the fix worked

The site detects your voice; if not, see the microphone lesson.

If it still does not work

If it still receives no sound, use Lesson 33 to check the Windows input device.

Chrome and websites

Lesson 10 Text on a website looks too large

What the problem means

The browser zoom may have changed accidentally.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click anywhere on the affected webpage away from a text box. What you should see: The page is active.

2. Hold Ctrl and press the zero key on the number row. What you should see: Chrome restores page zoom to 100 percent.

3. If you need larger text, hold Ctrl and press the plus key once. What you should see: The page becomes larger.

4. Repeat once at a time until comfortable, or use Ctrl and minus to reduce it. What you should see: You can adjust without losing the page edges.

Check whether the fix worked

Text becomes comfortable to read without cutting off page controls.

If it still does not work

If everything in Windows is oversized, use the display scale lesson instead.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 11 Wi-Fi is disconnected

What the problem means

The computer may not be connected to your router.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the network, speaker, or battery area near the clock in the lower right. What you should see: Quick settings opens.

2. If Wi-Fi is off, click its button to turn it on. What you should see: Wi-Fi becomes available.

3. Click the arrow beside the Wi-Fi button. What you should see: Nearby networks are listed.

4. Click your own network name. What you should see: Connection options appear.

5. Click Connect. If asked, enter your Wi-Fi password and click Next. What you should see: Windows attempts to join the network.

6. Open a familiar website. What you should see: You can test actual internet access.

Check whether the fix worked

The network says Connected and a familiar website opens.

If it still does not work

If the network says Connected but websites fail, continue with Lesson 12.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 12 Wi-Fi says connected but websites fail

What the problem means

The router may be reachable while internet access is unavailable.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open two familiar websites in separate browser tabs. What you should see: You can check whether more than one website fails.

2. On your phone, connect to the same Wi-Fi and try a website. What you should see: You can compare another device on the same network.

3. On the PC, click the network area near the clock. What you should see: Quick settings opens.

4. Turn Wi-Fi off, wait about five seconds, then turn it on. What you should see: The wireless connection restarts.

5. Reconnect to your own network and try the website again. What you should see: You can test whether reconnecting helped.

Check whether the fix worked

If all devices fail, focus on the router or provider; if only the PC fails, continue PC diagnosis.

If it still does not work

If every device fails, check your router or internet provider. If only the PC fails, use the Windows network diagnostic steps in Lesson 20.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 13 Only one website is unreachable

What the problem means

The site may be down or its address may be wrong.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open a new Chrome tab with the plus sign beside the tabs. What you should see: A blank tab appears.

2. Type a different familiar website address and press Enter. What you should see: You can check whether the internet works generally.

3. Return to the failing site and check the address for spelling mistakes. What you should see: You can correct a wrong address.

4. Press Ctrl and R to reload. What you should see: The site tries again.

5. Press Ctrl, Shift, and N together, then try the site in that Incognito window. What you should see: You can compare a different browser session.

Check whether the fix worked

Other websites work; record the exact error on the failing one.

If it still does not work

If the site alone fails, record the error and retry later. A single site failure does not prove your router is broken.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 14 Airplane mode blocks connections

What the problem means

Airplane mode disables wireless connections.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the network area beside the Windows clock. What you should see: Quick settings opens.

2. Find Airplane mode. What you should see: You can read whether it is on.

3. If it is on, click the Airplane mode button once. What you should see: Airplane mode switches off.

4. Click Wi-Fi to turn it on, then click its arrow. What you should see: The network list appears.

5. Choose your network and click Connect. What you should see: Windows reconnects.

Check whether the fix worked

The Wi-Fi list is visible and a website opens.

If it still does not work

If Airplane mode is already off, do not toggle other settings randomly. Check the Wi-Fi lesson.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 15 The wrong Wi-Fi network is selected

What the problem means

A saved nearby network may connect automatically.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the network area near the Windows clock. What you should see: Quick settings opens.

2. Click the arrow next to Wi-Fi. What you should see: Network names appear.

3. Read the name marked Connected. What you should see: You identify the current network.

4. Click your own network name. What you should see: Its connection options appear.

5. Click Connect and enter its password if asked. What you should see: Windows switches to your network.

Check whether the fix worked

The connected name matches your router and the internet works.

If it still does not work

If it keeps choosing another network, disconnect that network and clear its Connect automatically choice.

Internet and Wi-Fi

Lesson 16 Wi-Fi password is rejected

What the problem means

The password may contain a mistyped character or may have changed.

Fix it one step at a time

6. Click Next. What you should see: Windows attempts the connection.

3. Check that Caps Lock is off. What you should see: You avoid accidental uppercase letters.

4. Type the password carefully once, using the show password icon only if private. What you should see: You can spot a typing error.

5. If rejected, use Forgot password rather than guessing repeatedly. What you should see: The recovery process begins.

Check whether the fix worked

You sign in or receive a legitimate reset message.

If it still does not work

A Windows PIN, email password, and website password can be different. Note which account is failing.

Windows and accounts

Lesson 48 A suspicious pop-up says the PC is infected

What the problem means

A webpage can display alarming messages that imitate system warnings.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Do not click inside the warning or call its phone number. What you should see: You avoid responding to a webpage’s alarming claim.

2. Click the X on that browser tab. What you should see: The page closes if responsive.

3. If it cannot close, press Ctrl, Shift, and Esc together. What you should see: Task Manager opens.

4. Select Google Chrome under Processes and click End task. What you should see: Chrome closes; unsaved browser work may be lost.

5. Reopen Chrome without restoring that warning tab. What you should see: You can browse normally again.

6. Click Start, type Windows Security, and click the matching app in the results. What you should see: Windows Security opens.

7. Click Virus & threat protection. What you should see: Windows shows its protection provider and scan options.

8. If Microsoft Defender is active, click Quick scan. If another provider is listed, open that provider’s own scan tool. What you should see: You scan with the antivirus that actually protects this computer.

Check whether the fix worked

The pop-up is gone and you can review the scan result in Windows Security.

If it still does not work

If you installed software or gave remote access after the warning, disconnect that session and seek help promptly. A fake warning by itself does not establish an infection.

Windows and accounts

Lesson 49 A Windows notification keeps appearing

What the problem means

An app or website may have permission to send alerts.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the Windows Start button on the taskbar. What you should see: The Start menu opens.

2. Click Settings. If it is not visible, type Settings and click the Settings app in the results. What you should see: The Windows Settings window opens.

3. Click System. What you should see: The System settings appear.

4. Click Notifications. What you should see: The Notifications settings appear.

5. Scroll to the list of app senders. What you should see: Notification sources appear.

6. Find the app named in the unwanted notification. What you should see: You identify its own switch.

7. Turn off that app’s notification switch. What you should see: Its notifications are disabled.

Check whether the fix worked

That sender stops alerting while other notifications still work.

If it still does not work

For a website notification sent through Chrome, remove the site’s permission in Lesson 54 rather than disabling all Chrome alerts.

Windows and accounts

Lesson 50 Windows shows the wrong date or time

What the problem means

A wrong time zone or unsynchronized clock can show an incorrect time and cause some sign-in or certificate errors.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the Windows Start button on the taskbar. What you should see: The Start menu opens.

2. Click Settings. If it is not visible, type Settings and click the Settings app in the results. What you should see: The Windows Settings window opens.

3. Click Time & language. What you should see: The Time & language settings appear.

4. Click Date & time. What you should see: The Date & time settings appear.

5. Read the current date, time, and time zone. What you should see: You can compare them with the actual local time.

6. Turn Set time automatically on if your computer has internet access. What you should see: Windows can synchronize its clock.

7. Check Time zone; for Helena, Arkansas choose Central Time if it is wrong. What you should see: The local time zone is correct.

8. Click Sync now if shown. What you should see: Windows requests a time update.

Check whether the fix worked

Windows shows the correct local date, time, and time zone after synchronization.

If it still does not work

If the clock repeatedly resets after shutdown, note the pattern and seek hardware support. An incorrect clock can also interfere with website sign-ins.

More browser problems

Lesson 51 Chrome says it needs an update

What the problem means

An older browser can have compatibility problems with websites.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open Chrome and click the three dots in the upper right. What you should see: The browser menu opens.

2. Point to Help, then click About Google Chrome. What you should see: Chrome shows its version and checks for an update.

3. Wait while the check finishes. What you should see: You see either an update progress message or that Chrome is up to date.

4. If Relaunch appears, save any browser work and click Relaunch. What you should see: Chrome closes and reopens with the update.

5. Return to the website that was having trouble. What you should see: You can test its behavior again.

Check whether the fix worked

The About page says Chrome is up to date and you retested the original problem.

If it still does not work

If updating fails, record the error. Do not download a browser update from a random pop-up.

More browser problems

Lesson 52 You closed a browser tab by mistake

What the problem means

Chrome can often reopen a recently closed tab.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click inside the Chrome window. What you should see: Chrome is the active app.

2. Hold Ctrl and Shift, then press T. What you should see: The last closed tab reopens.

3. Repeat the shortcut once if you need the tab closed before that one. What you should see: The next recently closed tab returns.

4. Check the page address before continuing your work. What you should see: You confirm the correct page.

Check whether the fix worked

The intended tab is visible again.

If it still does not work

Incognito tabs are not recovered this way. Reopening a tab may not recover an unsaved form.

More browser problems

Lesson 53 A website keeps asking you to sign in

What the problem means

Incognito mode or site cookie settings may prevent a session from being kept.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Look at the top of the Chrome window for an Incognito label. What you should see: You can identify a private window.

2. If private, open a regular Chrome window from its icon. What you should see: You can try a normal session.

3. Open the official website and sign in once. What you should see: You have a fresh regular session.

4. Open another tab for the same site. What you should see: You can check whether it still recognizes you.

5. If it signs you out again, note whether it happens immediately or only after closing Chrome. What you should see: You have a pattern to investigate.

Check whether the fix worked

The site keeps the session during your test, or you have a clear repeatable sign-out pattern.

If it still does not work

Some sites intentionally expire sessions. Check cookie permissions for the affected site rather than turning off all browser privacy protection.

More browser problems

Lesson 54 A website sends unwanted notifications

What the problem means

A site may have been given permission to show alerts.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open Google Chrome. What you should see: A browser window appears.

2. Click the three dots in the upper right corner. What you should see: The Chrome menu opens.

3. Click Settings. What you should see: A Settings tab opens.

4. Click Privacy and security in the Settings menu. What you should see: The Privacy and security page appears.

5. Click Site settings in the Settings menu. What you should see: The Site settings page appears.

6. Click Notifications. What you should see: Notification permissions appear.

7. Find the unwanted site in the allowed list. What you should see: You identify the specific sender.

8. Click the three dots beside that site and choose Block or Remove. What you should see: Its permission is changed.

9. Close the Settings tab and continue browsing. What you should see: You can check whether those alerts stop.

Check whether the fix worked

That site no longer sends unwanted notifications.

If it still does not work

If the sender is absent, inspect the Windows notification’s app name; it may be coming from another program.

More browser problems

Lesson 55 A legitimate pop-up window is blocked

What the problem means

Some trusted sites use a separate window for a document or sign-in.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Open the trusted page and repeat the action that should open its window. What you should see: Chrome may show a blocked pop-up icon near the address bar.

2. Click that blocked pop-up icon if it appears. What you should see: Chrome lists the blocked window and options.

3. Select the specific blocked link to open it, or allow pop-ups for this trusted site only. What you should see: The intended window opens.

4. Complete the task and close the extra window. What you should see: You return to the original page.

Check whether the fix worked

The expected document or sign-in window appears.

If it still does not work

Do not allow pop-ups for an unknown advertising site. If no icon appears, the problem may belong to the website.

More browser problems

Lesson 56 A video on a webpage has no sound

What the problem means

The video player or the browser tab may be muted even when Windows sound works.

Fix it one step at a time

1. Click the video’s play button. What you should see: The video begins playing.

2. Look for a speaker icon inside the video player. What you should see: You can see its own mute control.

3. Click the speaker icon if muted and raise the player’s volume. What you should see: The player is no longer muted.
